stories.head: Could Loggers Lane flood again? High tides and storm surge peak Thursday
stories.dek: Environment Canada says coastal water in Squamish could rise each day this week at high tide, peaking Thursday, November 26, as storm surge lines up with king tides. In December 2022, similar conditions flooded downtown around Loggers Lane and set a record at Point Atkinson, the nearest tide gauge.
gist: Environment Canada warns that very high tides and storm waves could cause coastal flooding in Squamish this week, with water highest on Thursday.
In 2022, high water flooded downtown from Victoria Street south to Cattermole Slough, between Loggers Lane and Third Avenue.
A federal scientist says it is too early to know if water will reach the 2022 record, and tides around Christmas will be even higher.
Keep well back from high water, and sign up for District emergency alerts at Squamish.ca/alert.

tides.note: Point Atkinson records: CBC News, Dec. 27, 2022. This week's prediction: meteorologist Jason Ross via The Squamish Chief, which does not name the station for this figure.

surge.title: Separate things that push water above the tides, in cm (not added together)
surge.note: 2022 storm surge and El Niño effect: Bill Merryfield, Environment and Climate Change Canada, via The Squamish Chief. This week's forecast: Environment Canada coastal flooding statement. Upper end of each range shown. Each bar is a separate driver; they should not be added together.

stories.take: Keep well back from high water through the peak on Thursday, November 26, and sign up for District emergency alerts at Squamish.ca/alert.
stories.body:
[[glance]]

## What is happening

Environment Canada has a coastal flooding statement for much of the B.C. coast, including Squamish, for high tides on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, November 24 to 26. Deep low pressure systems offshore will bring storm surge and large waves during a run of king tides. Water could reach 20 to 50 cm above the highest astronomical tides (the highest tides from the moon and sun alone), and is expected to rise day over day, [The Squamish Chief reported](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/environment-canada-warns-of-flood-risk-in-squamish-similar-to-2022-event-13053913).

The statement [may be upgraded to a coastal flooding warning](https://www.squamishchief.com/highlights/vancouver-weather-flooding-king-tide-nov-2026-13053133) for some regions. Heavy rain is also forecast on the B.C. coast, with [100 to 200 mm depending on location](https://www.nationalobserver.com/2026/11/24/news/storm-surge-king-tides-converge-raise-flooding-risk-bc-coast). Check our [today page](/today/) for river levels, Highway 99 and conditions right now.

December may bring more risk. Bill Merryfield, a research scientist with Environment and Climate Change Canada, said tides around Christmas will be 2 to 3 cm higher than in December 2022, and El Niño is probably adding about 30 to 40 cm right now.

## How close to the record?

Meteorologist Jason Ross told The Squamish Chief the king tides could reach a predicted 5.058 m (16.6 ft). The record at Point Atkinson in West Vancouver, the nearest tide gauge to Squamish, is [5.70 m, set December 27, 2022](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/rain-snow-high-tide-flooding-bc-1.6698363). It beat 5.61 m from 1982. The source does not name the station for the 5.058 m figure, so the exact gap to the record cannot be worked out.

[[bars tides]]
Merryfield said a storm surge on top of this week's tides could bring water close to that record, but "it's probably too early to say whether that will occur."

## What happened in 2022

On December 27, 2022, water from Howe Sound spilled onto Loggers Lane and flooded some businesses and homes. The flooded area ran [from Victoria Street south to Cattermole Slough, between Loggers Lane and Third Avenue](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2022/12/27/crews-deal-with-flooding-downtown-majority-businesses-are-open/). Water went [several hundred metres inland](https://squamish.ca/projects-plans-and-initiatives/projects-and-initiatives-original/annual-flood-protection-upgrades/) and [seeped into The Main condo complex](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/high-tides-flood-downtown-core-6300605). The District said the [lack of a sea dike](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/who-will-protect-squamish-from-the-floods-6313184) was a major factor.

Merryfield said the 2022 flood was mostly caused by storm surge. When a storm passes, air pressure drops, which tends to pull the water level up. Winds blowing water onshore add to it. In 2022 that surge added about 70 cm on top of a king tide. There was also 200 mm of rain over five or six days, which may have limited how much of the seawater coming over the shore the soil could absorb.

[[bars surge]]
## Why the water is higher this year

- King tides come late in the year at full or new moon, when the Earth is closest to the sun and the moon is closest to the Earth.
- During El Niño, coastal winds blow more strongly from south to north, pushing water toward shore.
- Merryfield said the larger influence is likely a Kelvin wave: a pulse of raised sea level that probably began about three months ago in the equatorial Pacific, towards the Asian side, and travelled 20,000 to 25,000 km at about 10 km/h.

## The downtown sea dike

The District is building a [200 m sea dike at X̱wún̓eḵw Park](https://squamish.ca/projects-plans-and-initiatives/projects-and-initiatives/xwunekw-park-sea-dike/) on Loggers Lane, along the high water mark. A federal grant of [nearly $4.05 million](https://www.nsnews.com/local-news/district-of-squamish-receives-funding-for-sea-dike-3351571) helps pay for it. It is designed for [one metre of sea level rise by 2100](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/news/district-of-squamish-receives-4-million-grant-for-downtown-flood-protection-improvements/).

- 2017: District adopts a flood plan for its [21 km dike system](https://squamish.ca/sustainability-and-green-living/climate-action/climate-action/local-action/adaptation/)
- 2023: [earlier target](https://squamish.ca/sustainability-and-green-living/climate-action/climate-action/local-action/adaptation/) to build the new sea dike
- August 1, 2024: [Fisheries and Oceans Canada approval](https://squamish.ca/projects-plans-and-initiatives/projects-and-initiatives/xwunekw-park-sea-dike/)
- October 24, 2024: [call for construction proposals posted](https://squamish.ca/projects-plans-and-initiatives/projects-and-initiatives/xwunekw-park-sea-dike/)
- [Contract awarded to Jacob Bros Construction](https://squamish.ca/projects-plans-and-initiatives/projects-and-initiatives/xwunekw-park-sea-dike/) (no date given)
- 2026: [target finish](https://opendata-squamish.hub.arcgis.com/datasets/dike-upgrades/about), after a 2025 start

We could not confirm whether the new dike is finished, or its final cost.

## Staying safe

- The District says it is monitoring the situation.
- Keep well back from high water and be aware that waves may be significant. "Water levels can increase rapidly," the District says.
- We found no published high tide times for Squamish. Sign up at [Squamish.ca/alert](https://squamish.ca/alert) for District alerts.
- In 2022 the District ran a [sandbag station](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2022/12/27/crews-deal-with-flooding-downtown-majority-businesses-are-open/) at the north end of Brennan Park Recreation Centre (Ball Field #5). We found no sandbag notice this week.
- See our [flood protection](/issues/flood-protection/) page.

stories.head: Police clock 208 km/h in a 90 zone near Squamish. Here's the penalty
stories.dek: Police say a driver was going 208 km/h in a 90 km/h zone on Highway 99 near Squamish. BC Highway Patrol says the 22 year old man from California was stopped southbound at 5:10 p.m. on November 1. He was given a $483 ticket, which he can dispute, and his 2016 BMW was impounded for seven days.
gist: Police say a young driver from California went 208 km/h on Highway 99 near Squamish, where the limit is 90 km/h.
He was given a $483 ticket, the top fine for this kind of speeding, and his car was taken away for seven days.
In B.C., going 118 km/h over the limit brings the same fine as going 61 over.
A ticket is not a conviction, and it is not known whether he paid it or plans to fight it.

stories.take: In B.C., a first excessive speeding ticket brings a seven day impound, and a second offence within two years brings a 30 day impound. The fine is $368 for more than 40 km/h over and $483 for more than 60 over, [the Province says](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/transportation/driving-and-cycling/roadsafetybc/high-risk/speed).
stories.body:
[[glance]]

## What happened

A BC Highway Patrol officer was on Highway 99 near Squamish at 5:10 p.m. on November 1 when he saw a blue BMW heading south much faster than other traffic. He checked its speed with a police laser. The reading was 208 km/h in a 90 km/h zone. That is 118 km/h over the limit, about 2.3 times the limit (our arithmetic). The driver was a 22 year old man from California, driving a 2016 BMW.

[[bars overlimit]]
## What the driver got

He was given an excessive speed ticket under section 148(1) of the BC Motor Vehicle Act, with a fine of $483. His 2016 BMW was impounded for seven days.

The speed is alleged, as The Squamish Chief reports. A ticket is not a conviction. A driver has 30 days to dispute it, and if they do not, the courts find them guilty, [according to the Province](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/transportation/driving-and-cycling/roadsafetybc/high-risk/speed). If his 30 days started on November 1, they would run to about December 1 (our arithmetic).

## Why 118 over costs the same as 61 over

B.C. calls it excessive speeding when a driver goes more than 40 km/h over the limit. Police issue about [10,000 of these tickets a year](https://www.grsproadsafety.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Excessive-Speeding-and-Careless-Driving...ences-of-Unsafe-Driving-RoadSafetyBC1.pdf) across B.C. The [Province's rules](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/transportation/driving-and-cycling/roadsafetybc/high-risk/speed) set the fine at $368 for more than 40 over and $483 for more than 60 over, plus three penalty points. So $483 is the highest fine for this ticket.

[[bars fines]]
- A seven day impound is the standard penalty for a first offence. A second offence within two years brings a 30 day impound, [the Province says](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/transportation/driving-and-cycling/roadsafetybc/high-risk/speed).
- In September 2025, BC Highway Patrol said a ticket plus at least three years of high risk driving premiums comes to [almost $2,500](https://rcmp.ca/en/bc/bchp/news/2025/09/one-week-60-impounds-excessive-speeding-and-impairment-spikes-sea-sky). ICBC charges a [Driver Risk Premium](https://icbc.com/driver-licensing/tickets/Driver-Risk-Premium) for excessive speeding convictions.
- It is not known whether points or premiums apply to a driver from California.

## What police say

Michael McLaughlin of BC Highway Patrol said in a news release: "Even by the standards of the Sea to Sky Highway, this is a terribly dangerous speed. Visitors to B.C. are expected to understand and obey our traffic laws."

"No matter whether it's locals or visitors, treating the Sea to Sky like the Autobahn has got to stop," he said. He linked dangerous driving to deadly collisions that shut the highway for hours at a time.

## How often this happens

Speeding cases on the corridor:

- July 2025: a 21 year old from Burnaby was clocked at [194 km/h in an 80 zone](https://www.nsnews.com/local-news/burnaby-driver-clocked-at-194-kmh-caught-by-motorcycle-patrol-near-squamish-10983279) near Lions Bay.
- Christmas Day 2025: one officer [impounded 14 speeders](https://rcmp.ca/en/bc/bchp/news/2025/12/4348912) on Highway 99.
- Victoria Day long weekend 2026: the Squamish Highway Patrol unit issued [212 violation tickets and 66 excessive speed tickets](https://rcmp.ca/en/bc/bchp/news/2026/05/4353342). That set a long weekend record, beating 60 impounds over Labour Day 2025.
- July 2026: a 22 year old learner rider was clocked at [177 km/h in an 80 zone](https://rcmp.ca/en/bc/bchp/news/2026/07/4355038) near Furry Creek.

Separately, Sea to Sky RCMP told Squamish council there were 355 vehicle crashes in 2025, up from 295 in 2024, [The Squamish Chief reported](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/violent-crime-highway-collisions-rise-in-squamish-rcmp-says-12308567). There is no information linking this driver to those numbers.

[[bars crashes]]
The RCMP also told council it handed out 457 highway tickets in 2025. The Chief reported a figure of 527 by May 2026, but it is not clear what period that number covers.

ICBC counted [167 crashes between Vancouver and Whistler in 2024](https://globalnews.ca/news/11766800/sea-to-sky-highway-safer-crashes/), about one every two days. The RCMP and ICBC counts come from different agencies covering different areas, so they should not be compared. Across B.C., speed is a factor in more than 2,400 crashes a year and causes an average of 91 deaths, [ICBC says](https://icbc.com/road-safety/crashes-happen/speed).

## What residents can do

Highway 99 is a provincial highway, but Sea to Sky RCMP report to Squamish council once a year on local policing, including highway tickets and crashes. The last update was on May 19, 2026. Our guide to [how council works](/how-council-works/) explains how to follow meetings and share views with council members such as [Mayor Sean Easton](/council/sean-easton/). See also our pages on [transit and Highway 99](/issues/transit-and-highway-99/) and [policing and safety](/issues/policing-and-safety/), and [today](/today/) for highway conditions.

## What is not known

- Whether the driver paid or disputed the ticket, or how B.C. collects a fine from a California resident.
- What the impound cost, or whether the car was a rental.
- The exact spot beyond "near Squamish," and why the news came out 23 days after the stop.

The Squamish Chief [reported the story](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/california-driver-caught-speeding-at-208-kmh-on-sea-to-sky-highway-13053131).

stories.head: Squamish Nation: 200+ homes neared or began building; Elders Village plan
stories.dek: More than 200 new Squamish Nation homes neared or entered construction in the year to March 2026, and plans began for a Squamish Valley Elders Village. The Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish Nation) released its 2025/26 Annual Report on November 24. Members will hear it at the Annual General Meeting on November 28 and 29.
gist: The Squamish Nation has shared its yearly report for April 2025 to March 2026.
It lists more than 200 new Nation homes, though it does not say where, plus a new Language Nest and Elders Village plans in the Squamish Valley.
The report does not list the more than 20 planned projects, and it does not say when the Elders Village will be built.
Members can hear the report at the Annual General Meeting on November 28 and 29, in person or online.

stories.take: Squamish Nation Members can hear the 2025/26 Annual Report at the Annual General Meeting on November 28 and 29 at CJMC, Totem Hall or online, anyone can read the full report on the Nation's website, and we found no public process for non-members to comment.
stories.body:
[[glance]]

The Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish Nation) released its 2025/26 syétsem tl’a syel̓ánem, or Annual Report, on November 24. It covers April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2026, and shares the Nation's financial statements and its work across government, departments and entities. In the Squamish Valley, plans were set in motion for an Elders Village, which a 2024 Nation plan put on [land near Totem Hall](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2024/11/27/elders-village-food-hub-housing-part-of-squamish-nation-plan-for-land-near-totem-hall/).

## In the Squamish Valley

- **Language Nest:** A new one opened in the Squamish Valley. The release does not say where it is or explain what it offers.
- **Community Plan:** The Squamish Valley Community Plan was unveiled. It is a [10-year plan shown to members at Totem Hall on December 9, 2025 and approved in February 2026](https://www.squamishchief.com/in-the-community/looking-back-paddling-forward-what-is-the-squamish-nation-squamish-valley-community-plan-12551944). Its planned projects include a Valley transportation system, a treatment centre, a hotel and a business park. The Nation's Valley [reaches south to Porteau Cove and across Howe Sound to Ḵw'émḵw'em, and a 12-person advisory group of Valley residents gave input](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/squamish-nation-unveils-first-10-year-valley-plan-11590057). The plan [feeds into the 2026-2030 Strategic Plan](https://www.squamish.net/community-initiatives/land-development-strategies/).
- **Elders Village:** The Nation's [elder care page](https://www.squamish.net/community-initiatives/land-planning/elder-care/) says Council approved a business plan. It covers 26 Elder homes with long-term care and assisted living, a new Elders Centre, a traditional food hub, a childcare centre and more than 100 homes for several generations. We found no budget, funding source or start date.
- **Future projects:** More than 20 major projects are being planned across the North Shore and the Squamish Valley over the next five years. The report does not list them.

[[bars elders]]
## Housing

More than 200 new Nation homes neared or entered construction during the year. The report does not say where they are, so they may be on the North Shore, in the Valley or both. The Nation's April 2024 plan aimed to [start building 600 Hiy̓ám̓ rental homes by the end of 2025](https://www.squamish.net/community-initiatives/land-planning/600-homes/). The release does not give a running total.

- Last year's report said Hiy̓ám̓ would be [breaking ground on another 200 units](https://www.squamish.net/syetsem-tla-syel%CC%93anem-annual-report-2024-5/). These may be the same homes.
- The Nation's [600 homes page](https://www.squamish.net/community-initiatives/land-planning/600-homes/) says 305 homes had broken ground, a 45% increase in the Nation's housing supply.
- A [March 2024 study](https://www.squamish.net/community-initiatives/land-planning/600-homes/) found 885 more homes are needed over five years. About 1,650 members living off reserve would like to return. The Nation's top priority is housing all members within 25 years.
- The latest finished Valley project we found is [27 Hiy̓ám̓ homes at 41139 Government Road](https://hiyamhousing.com/project-government-road/). Tenants began moving in in February 2024. Hiy̓ám̓ takes applications separately from the Nation's housing list.
- In 2023 the District of Squamish counted [about 120 Nation single-detached houses in Squamish, plus a 10-plex and a 13-plex in Brackendale](https://squamish.ca/assets/Affordable-Housing-General/230418SquamishHNRFINAL.pdf).

[[bars homes]]
More on local housing: [our housing page](/issues/housing/).

## Other highlights

- **Health and safety:** People Services on Wheels launched. Ha7lh Sḵwalwnawtxw Siyích’em (Healthy Hub Siyích’em) opened. Community Safety Team patrol hours were extended.
- **Recreation and Elders:** Ḵw’eshḵw’shétsutay̓ (Playing Place) opened. Work on the expanded North Shore Elders Centre [began in October 2025, and Elders should start moving back by the end of January 2027](https://www.squamish.net/elders-centre-expansion-on-schedule/).
- **International Plaza:** On September 10, 2025, Nch’ḵay̓ [bought CAPREIT's land lease interest for $54.2 million, not counting transaction costs](https://www.capreit.ca/capreit-completes-sale-of-international-plaza-to-nch%E1%B8%B5ay-development-corporation/). The towers are at [1959-1999 Marine Drive in North Vancouver](https://www.nsnews.com/real-estate-news/squamish-nation-buys-north-vancouver-apartment-complex-for-542m-11206470), and the purchase used a commercial mortgage through Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
- **Sen̓áḵw:** This Vancouver project has about [6,000 rental homes, with 300 set aside for Squamish families](https://www.npr.org/2026/04/09/nx-s1-5773346/in-vancouver-squamish-nation-builds-what-many-cities-struggle-to-lots-of-housing). After developer Westbank sold its stake, [the pension fund OPTrust and the Nation own Phases 1 and 2 equally](https://www.biv.com/news/westbank-sells-stake-in-massive-squamish-nation-housing-development-in-vancouver-11143764). The Nation now owns all of Phases 3 and 4.
- **Money:** Regular income the Nation earns itself went up, through lease rate reviews, property renewals and additions to the tax roll. The release gives no total revenue, surplus or debt.

## Where and when

- Annual General Meeting for Members: Saturday, November 28 and Sunday, November 29
- At CJMC, Totem Hall and online
- Printed reports will be available at the meeting
- The full report, and past reports, are online on the [Squamish Nation website](https://www.squamish.net/squamish-nation-2025-26-annual-report/)

## What we could not find

- The release does not explain what CJMC stands for.
- We found no source on any District of Squamish role in these projects.

stories.head: Monday fire at Mamquam Road business may be arson. Police want video
stories.dek: Squamish RCMP are treating a fire at a Garibaldi Estates business early Monday, November 23, as a possible arson. Squamish Fire Rescue called police to the 1800 block of Mamquam Road at about 3:50 a.m. Police want to hear from anyone with information, anyone who was in the area, or anyone with video from 3 to 4:30 a.m. They have not named the business.
gist: A business in the 1800 block of Mamquam Road in the Garibaldi Estates had a suspicious fire early Monday, November 23.
Police are treating it as a possible arson, which means they think it may have been set on purpose.
Police have not named the business, said how bad the damage is, or said whether anyone was hurt, and the investigation is in its early stages.
If you were in the area between 3 a.m. and 4:30 a.m. or have video, call 604-892-6100 and quote file 2026-10289.
stories.take: If you were near Mamquam Road between 3 and 4:30 a.m. on November 23 or have camera footage from then, call Squamish RCMP at 604-892-6100 and quote file 2026-10289.
stories.body:
[[glance]]

## What happened

The call came from Squamish Fire Rescue, which asked police to come to a suspicious fire at a business on Mamquam Road in the Garibaldi Estates, according to an RCMP news release [reported by The Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/possible-arson-investigation-underway-at-squamish-business-13051660).

After investigating at the scene, officers are treating the fire as a possible arson. Possible arson means police think the fire may have been set on purpose; they have not said why. Police say the investigation is in its early stages, and The Chief says its story is being updated. We will update this story as police release more.

## How to help police

Police are asking for help from anyone who:

- has information about the fire
- has video from a surveillance camera, dashcam or other vehicle camera
- was in the area between 3 a.m. and 4:30 a.m. on November 23

That window is 90 minutes long and starts about 50 minutes before Fire Rescue called police (our arithmetic), so police want footage from before the call too. If you have a home, business or dash camera facing Mamquam Road, check your footage from that window.

To reach police:

- Call the Squamish RCMP detachment at 604-892-6100
- Quote RCMP file number 2026-10289

## Timeline

- 3:00 a.m.: the window police want footage from opens
- About 3:50 a.m.: Squamish Fire Rescue calls the RCMP about a suspicious fire
- 4:30 a.m.: the footage window closes
- Monday night: The Chief sees plywood covering one of the windows

Source: The Squamish Chief, RCMP release, Nov 23, 2026.

## Which business

Police did not name the business. The Squamish Chief reported that online reports point to the Cloudburst Café at 1861 Mamquam Road, which is in the Squamish Town Hub. Police have not confirmed it is the business involved. Squamish Voters could not find a statement from the owners.

## What we don't know yet

News reports of the police release do not mention damage, injuries or suspects. Police have not said:

- how much damage there was
- whether anyone was inside or hurt
- whether the business will stay open
- what made them suspect arson
- whether fire investigators are working with them on the cause
- whether there are any suspects, or whether this is linked to anything else

Follow local police and safety news on our [policing and safety](/issues/policing-and-safety/) page, and news for the Garibaldi Estates and other areas on our [neighbourhoods](/neighbourhoods/) page.

stories.head: Squamish's Jeremy Valeriote won by 2,358 votes. Now he's one of two Greens
stories.dek: Squamish's member of the legislature, Jeremy Valeriote, sits in a two-member Green caucus across from a Conservative majority. He and Green Leader Emily Lowan were sworn in at the legislature in Victoria on Monday, November 23. The legislature does not sit again until spring.
gist: Jeremy Valeriote, the Green who represents Squamish in the provincial legislature, took his oath for a new term on Monday.
He won last month by 2,358 votes, and his share of the vote rose from 38.1 per cent in 2024 to 47.8 per cent.
The New Democrat vote in the riding fell from 7,213 to 2,561, while the Conservative vote slipped slightly.
In the Canadian Press report he did not say what he will push for on local issues, and the legislature does not meet again until spring.

stories.take: Valeriote stays Squamish's member of the legislature, and with no sitting until spring, residents can find his contact details at leg.bc.ca to raise local issues with him now.
stories.body:
[[glance]]
## A new term in a caucus of two
Jeremy Valeriote, the member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) for West Vancouver-Sea to Sky, was sworn in on Monday, November 23, in Victoria, along with Green Leader Emily Lowan, [The Canadian Press reported](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/bc-greens-including-leader-emily-lowan-sworn-in-as-legislators-in-victoria-13047286). Former federal Green leader Elizabeth May and former provincial Green MLA Adam Olsen attended. Lowan, 26, is newly elected in Saanich North and the Islands and won the party leadership a little over a year ago.

In the Canadian Press report he did not say what he will push for on Squamish issues such as housing, Highway 99 or Woodfibre LNG. His one quote was on climate change, which he said the Greens will focus on even as others may crowd it out. "It is an existential threat that we can't delay on," he said.

The riding covers Bowen Island, Lions Bay, Pemberton, Squamish, West Vancouver and Whistler, [according to BC Ballot](https://bcballot.ca/ridings/west-vancouver-sea-to-sky/). Contact details for MLAs are at [leg.bc.ca](https://www.leg.bc.ca/).

## How the vote went
In the October 24 snap election, Valeriote won by 2,358 votes with 47.8 per cent, up from 38.1 per cent in 2024, [BC Ballot shows](https://bcballot.ca/ridings/west-vancouver-sea-to-sky/). These numbers come from that tracker, not Elections BC. In 2020, Jordan Sturdy of BC United beat him by 60 votes, or 0.24 per cent, [Global News reported](https://globalnews.ca/news/10779144/bc-election-2024-results-west-vancouver-sea-to-sky/).

[[bars margin]]
[[bars result]]
The Green vote rose from 10,438 to 11,834, the Conservative vote slipped from 9,762 to 9,476, and the New Democrat vote fell from 7,213 to 2,561, [BC Ballot shows](https://bcballot.ca/ridings/west-vancouver-sea-to-sky/). This is only the second time the Greens have won the riding, [Pique reported](https://www.piquenewsmagazine.com/must-reads/jeremy-valeriote-re-elected-mla-in-west-vancouver-sea-to-sky-12935722).

[[bars change]]
## Where the Greens and Conservatives stand
Lowan said the Greens shared common ground with the Conservatives, when they were the Official Opposition, on emergency room closures, foreign ownership of farmland and B.C.'s "crumbling" infrastructure.

Climate is where they disagree most. Lowan says the government is going the wrong way by promising to double natural gas production and triple liquefied natural gas exports, [National Observer reported](https://nationalobserver.com/2026/11/23/news/bc-greens-take-oath-office-leader-lowan-laments-failed-climate-conference). See our [Woodfibre LNG](/issues/woodfibre-lng/) page. She said: "I meet British Columbians every day who are absolutely crushed by the status quo and don't think that the best use of public dollars is to empty out the purse for foreign-owned LNG and subsidize extractive corporations that, more often than not, rip-and-ship those profits overseas."

Premier Lorne Doerkson congratulated both Greens and said he looks forward to "finding common ground."

## Timeline
- November 19: 63 Conservative MLAs sworn in, [Daily Hive reported](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/bc-conservative-cabinet-minister-names-list-november-2026)
- November 20: Doerkson sworn in as premier, [the Globe and Mail reported](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-conservative-lorne-doerkson-sworn-bc-premier/)
- November 23: Greens sworn in
- Thursday, November 26: New Democrat MLAs sworn in, [National Observer reported](https://nationalobserver.com/2026/11/23/news/bc-greens-take-oath-office-leader-lowan-laments-failed-climate-conference)
- Spring: session opens with a throne speech, the speech where the government lays out its priorities; a new session cannot start without one. No date is set and there is no fall sitting, [CBC reported](https://ca.news.yahoo.com/incoming-b-c-conservative-government-023206393.html).

We could not confirm whether a party of two gets official party status or what roles Valeriote will hold. See also [climate and environment](/issues/climate-and-environment/) and [transit and Highway 99](/issues/transit-and-highway-99/).

stories.head: Mayor Easton says parking cuts aren't working. What he wants instead
stories.dek: Squamish's new mayor says letting new buildings have fewer parking stalls has made parking worse, because transit is still weak. Sean Easton told The Squamish Chief he wants residents to define what the town needs, with council's new strategic plan in the coming months setting goals to measure.
gist: New Mayor Sean Easton says cutting parking in new buildings has not worked in Squamish.
He says parking from new buildings spills onto neighbouring streets, and fewer stalls only make sense with much better transit.
He wants council to judge itself on real results, like homes people can afford, not on finished plans.
Council will write its plan for the next four years in the coming months, but no dates for it or for public input are set yet.

cleveland.note: Source: North Shore News, 2025. 20 home spaces plus 8 commercial spaces (our arithmetic). Council approved the cut for a $240,000 payment.

stories.take: Mayor Easton says council will set its direction in a strategic plan in the coming months; no dates for the plan or public input are set yet.
stories.body:
[[glance]]
## What he says isn't working
Letting new buildings have fewer parking stalls than the rules normally require is not working in Squamish, [Mayor Sean Easton](/council/sean-easton/) told The Squamish Chief at the Housing Central Conference in Vancouver last week.

The District's view has been that fewer stalls near bus routes encourages transit use and lowers emissions. Easton called that "an ideologically grounded approach" and says the parking challenge has gotten worse. We found no District data that proves or disproves that parking has gotten worse. He says parking needs from new buildings are "bleeding out into the community," and that less reliance on cars needs a more robust transit system. Many residents commute to the resort or to Vancouver, he says.

Asked about a recent Government Road proposal with far fewer stalls than bylaws normally require, he said many residents feel left out, and neighbours feel the effects without having a say. We have not checked whether provincial rules limit what council can require on parking near transit.

## When residents can weigh in
Easton says change will come through council's strategic plan, its four year list of priorities, written in the coming months with specific outcome measures to guide District staff. The [last plan](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/council/strategic-plan/) covered 2023 to 2026.

- No dates are set yet for the plan or for public input.
- Last time, the District [asked the public](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/district-of-squamish-strategic-plan-7091990) to comment on its draft.
- Follow our [parking](/issues/parking/), [housing](/issues/housing/) and [scorecard](/scorecard/) pages.

## How council has handled parking before
In July 2025, council let a [Cleveland Avenue building](https://www.nsnews.com/real-estate/more-rental-units-coming-to-downtown-squamishif-you-dont-own-a-car-10967161) drop all 20 required home spaces and all eight commercial spaces, for a payment of $240,000. A 2020 District [parking study](https://squamish.ca/assets/Parking/200226-DoS-Downtown-Parkade-Study.pdf) lists $15,000 per space; we could not find how the $240,000 was set.

[[bars cleveland]]
But in 2025 council also told one developer it could not support a [parking cut at University Highlands](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/councillors-not-willing-to-support-bold-parking-variance-for-university-highlands-development-10669687) because of a lack of transit. That is the same reason Easton gives now.

[[bars highlands]]
Early in 2026, [Northyards residents opposed](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2026/01/05/northyards-residents-oppose-parking-variance-development/) fewer spaces in a proposed six storey rental building on Aspen Road; we found no final decision. [BC Transit added weekday trips](https://www.bctransit.com/transit-service-expansion-in-squamish-2025-12-18/) to Route 1 Brackendale on January 4, 2026. A [Sea to Sky regional bus](https://www.bctransit.com/potential-transit-service-options-identified-for-sea-to-sky-corridor/) was studied in 2017, and the District [once said](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/news/sea-to-sky-governments-make-progress-toward-regional-transit/) work was underway to start service in fall 2019. We found no current launch date.

## Results, not checklists
Counting finished tasks is "a false proxy to success," Easton says, meaning it does not show whether life got better. He pointed to a report saying the Housing Action Plan was complete or 95 per cent done, helped by the federal Housing Accelerator Fund, which gave the District [over $7 million](https://www.cmhc-schl.gc.ca/media-newsroom/news-releases/2024/helping-build-more-homes-faster-squamish) in 2024 to speed up more than 200 homes over three years. He called Squamish the second most expensive community in the province; we could not confirm that or the 95 per cent. He said vacancy is zero; the long term rental rate was [0.2 per cent](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2026/03/24/short-term-rentals-drop-but-squamishs-housing-crunch-persists/) in March 2026.

He wants residents to say what they need, then council to set goals and measure them. He says satisfaction in the District's own survey is declining. In the [2025 survey](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2025/06/25/squamish-residents-worry-growth-is-outrunning-local-services/), a separate question found 58 per cent said things were worse than five years ago. The top issue, at 38 per cent, was services keeping up with growth. Parking was grouped with traffic and transit in one answer, which ranked third.

[[bars survey]]
## Background
Easton beat Jenna Stoner by [175 votes](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/council/election/), with about 42 per cent of votes for mayor (our arithmetic). Turnout was about 45 per cent. At the conference he led a session with Zero Ceiling and DWIFT Housing Society, two housing nonprofits he is connected with. [Read the full interview](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/qa-new-squamish-mayor-makes-the-case-for-resident-centred-governance-13045060).

stories.head: Man charged with murder in death of Lions Bay actor Stewart McLean
stories.dek: Six months after Lions Bay actor and producer Stewart McLean, 45, was reportedly last seen at his home, a man is charged in his death. Nathan Ambros Neima, 35, of New Westminster, was arrested November 21. He was charged the same day with one count of second-degree murder.
gist: A New Westminster man, 35, was arrested November 21 and charged with second-degree murder in the death of Lions Bay actor Stewart McLean.
Squamish RCMP led the first investigation after McLean, 45, was reported missing in May, and the accused is now held until a possible bail hearing.
In May, the homicide team said it believed the death was an isolated incident.
It is sharing no more details now that the case is before the courts.

glance.v: Nathan Ambros Neima, 35, of New Westminster
Life in prison, no parole for at least 10 to 25 years

timeline.title: Days after Stewart McLean was last seen on May 15
timeline.note: Dates from The Squamish Chief and RCMP/IHIT; day counts are our arithmetic.

stories.take: The accused is in custody, and anyone with information can still call the homicide tip line at 1-877-551-4448.
stories.body:
[[glance]]

## What happened

A man has been charged in the death of Stewart McLean, a 45 year old Lions Bay resident. The Squamish Chief [reported the charge](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/new-westminster-man-charged-with-murder-in-death-of-lions-bay-resident-12301725) on November 23.

The Squamish Chief names the accused as Nathan Ambros Neima, 35, of New Westminster. He was arrested on Saturday, November 21, and charged the same day. The BC Prosecution Service approved one count of second-degree murder against him.

A charge is not a conviction. Neima is presumed innocent, and nothing has been proven in court.

In May, the Integrated Homicide Investigation Team said it believed the death was an isolated incident. Corporal Esther Tupper of the team now says the charge reflects "months of hard work and evidence gathering." The team offered condolences to McLean's family and friends. It says it will release no more information because the matter is before the courts.

## How the case unfolded

Lions Bay is about 20 kilometres northwest of Vancouver, [according to CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/stewart-mclean-homicide-unit-remains-9.7209461).

- May 15: McLean was reportedly last seen at his home in the [Brunswick Beach area of Lions Bay](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/stewart-mclean-homicide-unit-remains-9.7209461).
- May 18: Squamish RCMP received a report that he was missing. A friend, actor and acting coach Jeff Seymour, [raised the alarm](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/arts/article-remains-of-missing-actor-stewart-mclean-found-north-of-vancouver/) after hearing McLean had not shown up for a day of filming.
- May 20: The homicide team took over after Squamish RCMP found evidence that pointed to a homicide. Lions Bay Search and Rescue [began searching](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/arts/article-remains-of-missing-actor-stewart-mclean-found-north-of-vancouver/) that day.
- May 22: Police confirmed McLean's remains had been found in the Lions Bay area.
- November 21: A suspect was arrested and charged, 190 days after McLean was last seen (our count).

[[bars timeline]]
In May, investigators said they were reviewing CCTV footage and doing interviews to build a timeline of McLean's activities before May 15. The team thanked Squamish RCMP, the police dog service, forensic identification teams and Lions Bay Search and Rescue, and worked with the BC Coroners Service.

## Who Stewart McLean was

McLean, also known as Stew, was well known in the local film industry as an actor and producer. He was [born in Edmonton](https://hollywoodlife.com/feature/stewart-stew-mclean-virgin-river-character-5540617/). He appeared in Virgin River, which was shot in Squamish, playing [a barfly in a season 7 episode](https://hollywoodlife.com/feature/stewart-stew-mclean-virgin-river-character-5540617/). He was also in [Murder in a Small Town](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/stewart-mclean-homicide-unit-remains-9.7209461) and on [Arrow, Supernatural and The Irrational](https://www.eonline.com/news/1432279/virgin-rivers-stewart-mclean-missing-believed-to-be-homicide-victim). He often filmed around the Vancouver area, [including Bowen Island and Squamish](https://variety.com/2026/tv/news/stewart-mclean-missing-murder-actor-virgin-river-1236757234/).

## What comes next

- Neima is held in custody pending a possible bail application in B.C. Supreme Court.
- His next court appearance was set for Monday, November 23, at North Vancouver Provincial Court. What happened there has not been reported.
- Under the [Criminal Code](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/c-46/) (sections 469, 515(11) and 522), only a B.C. Supreme Court judge can grant bail on a murder charge, and the accused must show why he should be released.
- Anyone convicted of second-degree murder faces a mandatory life sentence, with no parole for at least 10 years. A judge can raise that to as much as 25 years ([Criminal Code](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/c-46/) sections 745 and 745.4).

## What is still not known

- How or when McLean died, or why.
- Whether the two men knew each other.
- Exactly where the remains were found.
- What happened at the November 23 court appearance, and the next court date.

## How to help

- Anyone with information can call the homicide team's tip line at 1-877-551-IHIT (4448).
- The IHIT file number is [2026-536](https://rcmp.ca/en/bc/ihit/news/2026/05/4353443).

More local safety news is on our [policing and safety](/issues/policing-and-safety/) page.

stories.head: Squamish's engineering head moves to Whistler. Her job is already posted
stories.dek: The person who oversaw more than $30 million a year in Squamish construction projects is leaving for Whistler. Sarah Baillie, the District of Squamish's director of engineering, is Whistler's new general manager of infrastructure services. Squamish posted her job on November 13. Her last day here has not been announced.
gist: Whistler has hired Sarah Baillie, who runs engineering for the District of Squamish, to lead its roads, utilities, wastewater treatment and building projects.
In Squamish she oversaw infrastructure planning, transportation, engineering for new development and more than $30 million a year in construction projects.
Her last day here, and who will fill in while Squamish hires, have not been announced.
The District has already posted her job and is also hiring a manager of capital projects.

stories.body:
[[glance]]

## What happened

The Resort Municipality of Whistler has hired Sarah Baillie, the District of Squamish's director of engineering, as its new general manager of infrastructure services. Whistler announced the hire in a [release on November 12](https://www.whistler.ca/news/release-whistler-hires-municipal-engineering-leader-to-head-infrastructure-services/). Squamish council minutes list her as Director Engineering [at a July 23, 2024 meeting](https://squamish.civicweb.net/document/242560/).

Still not announced: her last day in Squamish, her start date in Whistler, who is acting director of engineering, and when the District expects to fill the job. We found no statement from the District.

The story was written [by Luke Faulks of Pique Newsmagazine](https://www.piquenewsmagazine.com/local-news/whistler-names-squamish-engineering-director-former-olympian-to-senior-role-13009988) and also [ran in the Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/whistler-names-squamish-engineering-director-former-olympian-to-senior-role-13009988). [ReNew Canada reports](https://www.renewcanada.net/people-moves-november/) that she has joined Whistler, but gives no date.

## Squamish is already hiring

- November 12: Whistler announces the hire
- November 13: Squamish posts her job on [CivicJobs](https://www.civicjobs.ca/jobs?id=117316) and [Job Bank](https://www.jobbank.gc.ca/jobsearch/jobposting/50722131)
- November 21: the news runs in the Squamish Chief
- Before Thursday, November 26: applicants must apply

The District is also hiring a Manager of Capital Projects, listed on its [job postings page](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/careers/job-postings/), so two senior jobs on the engineering side are open at once.

## Her work in Squamish

Baillie oversaw infrastructure planning, transportation, development engineering and a yearly capital program of more than $30 million. A capital program is the money spent building and fixing things the town owns, such as roads, pipes and buildings. The release does not say which year that figure covers, or whether it means money budgeted or work done.

A November 2025 budget plan set [a planned capital budget of $42.7 million for 2026, or $348 million over 10 years](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/squamish-budget-2025-what-to-know-about-brennan-park-plans-and-more-11557723).

[[bars capital]]
Council adopted the District's first financial plan covering 10 years [on January 13, 2026](https://www.civicinfo.bc.ca/news?newsid=9674). It includes an [$82.2 million operating budget and projects tax increases averaging over 8% a year](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/update-tough-budget-squamish-council-adopts-first-decade-long-financial-plan-11710524).

[[bars budget]]
More on our [property taxes](/issues/property-taxes/), [flood protection](/issues/flood-protection/) and [growth and development](/issues/growth-and-development/) pages.

## Her new job

The release says she will be in charge of Whistler's roads, utilities, wastewater treatment and municipal construction projects. Whistler's [Infrastructure Services division](https://www.whistler.ca/municipal-services/divisions-working-groups/) covers Engineering Services, Road and Flood Protection, Utilities (Water and Sewer), the Waste Treatment Plant, Solid Waste and facility construction. She will report directly to chief administrative officer Chris Vick.

"She understands how infrastructure investments shape communities," said Whistler Mayor Jack Crompton.

"She brings a strong record of building teams, strengthening organizations and advancing major projects," Vick said.

Her priorities include planning infrastructure for the long term, asset management (keeping track of and caring for what the town owns) and planning for municipal buildings, to help Whistler maintain services while preparing for future growth. "My background is in municipal infrastructure, from planning and design through construction and delivery," Baillie said.

[Whistler's 2025 Statement of Financial Information](https://pub-rmow.escribemeetings.com/filestream.ashx?DocumentId=26139) lists $217,521 paid to the previous general manager, James Hallisey, in 2025. Baillie's salary has not been disclosed.

## Who she is

Baillie is a professional engineer and chartered civil engineer with a degree from Carleton University. She worked in consulting and municipal engineering in Canada and the United Kingdom. She has also overseen major facilities projects during a leadership secondment, a temporary assignment into a leadership role.

She was planning chief in emergency operations during the 2025 Dryden Creek wildfire, which brought a [local state of emergency](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/bc-wildfire-update-june-13-1.7560896) north of Squamish in June 2025. The fire reached [59.5 hectares and was classed as being held by June 14, 2025](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/news/dryden-creek-wildfire-update-june-14-2025/). The District [declared a Local Recovery Period on July 21, 2025](https://squamish.ca/public-safety-services/emergency-program/emergency-updates/dryden/).

She paddled for Canada in canoe slalom at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, listed as [Sarah Boudens, born in Pembroke, Ontario, in 1983](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Boudens), finishing [19th in women's single kayak](https://www.olympics.com/en/olympic-games/beijing-2008/results/canoe-slalom/k1-kayak-single-women). She is preparing for the 2027 Masters World Championships and has lived in Squamish with her family since 2018.
stories.social:
Sarah Baillie has run engineering for the District of Squamish, overseeing more than $30 million a year in construction projects. Now Whistler has hired her for a senior job, and she once paddled for Canada at the Beijing Olympics.

Squamish posted her job on November 13. Her last day here has not been announced, and neither has who covers the work in the meantime. Who fills in while Squamish hires? What we know so far:

stories.take: The school board will write to parents about electric bike rules, schools are not to store the bikes, and anyone can email comments on Woodfibre LNG's air permit, aiming for November 27.
stories.body:
[[glance]]
## What was decided
Trustees for School District No. 48 (Sea to Sky) agreed at their first regular meeting of the new term to write to parents about electric bikes, and to write to Woodfibre LNG and the BC Energy Regulator about the company's air permit. If you want to comment on that permit yourself, aim for November 27 and confirm the date with the regulator (see How to comment on the permit). The Squamish Chief [reported the meeting](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/sd48-trustees-call-for-stricter-air-emission-regulations-for-woodfibre-lng-13045150).

## The electric bike letter
Board chair April Lowe said electric bikes (e-bikes) came up often during the recent election, and there is a lot of confusion. She said many people answered "Really?" when she told them it is illegal for children under 16 to ride one. The provincial rule is a little more detailed: 14 for a light e-bike and 16 for a standard one (see below). Lowe said she often sees kids, even in elementary school, riding them, and that she is not suggesting a ban.

What else was said:
- At Garibaldi Highlands, the rule is that students get off and walk their e-bike, Lowe said.
- Some schools have been storing the bikes because they get stolen or vandalised during the school day, Lowe said.
- Superintendent Chris Nicholson said principals have been told not to store e-bikes in schools. On a request to buy racks for them, he said: "No."
- He said Don Ross worked with the RCMP to get the rules out, and the topic has been in parent newsletters.
- Vancouver Coastal Health is preparing materials for schools, and its medical health officer offered to speak to the Sea to Sky District Parent Advisory Council and to schools.

"I am terrified, and I'm saying this in public, for anyone who's listening," Nicholson said. He said he has seen multiple kids on a bike or scooter, no helmet, popping the curb into traffic. "We need the support of parents."

In 2025, Squamish RCMP reported more e-bike crashes with injuries, mostly involving youth, and the school district said it was running a summer education campaign. Vancouver Coastal Health's Dr. Brandon Yau said then that e-bikes are not meant for youth under 16 ([Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/are-e-bikes-safe-what-squamish-riders-and-officials-are-saying-11038825)). In a separate case, the district earlier wrote to the District of Squamish about traffic and parking safety at École Squamish Elementary ([Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/sea-to-sky-school-district-steps-in-over-parking-issues-at-squamish-elementary-9990307)).

Pemberton trustee Melissa Ronayne moved the motion, and Rebecca Barley, trustee for Squamish-Lillooet Regional District Area C, seconded it.

## What the provincial rules say
- Riders must be 14 or older for a light e-bike and 16 or older for a standard one. Parents must not knowingly let younger children ride ([Province of B.C.](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/transportation/driving-and-cycling/cycling/cycling-regulations-restrictions-rules/e-bikes)).
- No driver's licence or insurance is needed, but the age rule applies (same page).
- The regulation says a person under 16 "must not operate a standard e-bike on a highway" ([B.C. Reg. 64/2024](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/64_2024)). Whether that covers school grounds is not clear.
- Riders under 16 may not carry or tow a passenger (same regulation).
- Bike rules require all riders to wear a helmet on public roads; the fine is $29 ([Province of B.C.](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/transportation/driving-and-cycling/cycling/cycling-regulations-restrictions-rules)).

[[bars ages]]
Parents with questions about how their child's school handles e-bikes can ask the school directly.

## The Woodfibre LNG air permit
More on the project: [Woodfibre LNG](/issues/woodfibre-lng/).

Woodfibre LNG (liquefied natural gas) has applied for an air permit, called a Waste Discharge Authorization. The export plant needs it to move to its start-up phase. The application lists where emissions come from, including flaring, the steps to manage them, and air modelling for nearby communities.

The motion, passed unanimously: "that the Board of Education write a letter to Woodfibre LNG and the BC Energy Regulator requesting that the regulator applies stringent regulations for prioritizing public health of students and staff in relation to the Waste Discharge Authorization air permit application."

Trustee Celeste Bickford, who represents Squamish-Lillooet Regional District Area D, suggested it, and new Squamish trustee Leanne Roderick moved it. "The school district has a responsibility to advocate for the health, safety and well-being of students and staff who may be affected by the industrial air emissions," Bickford said. She said the board wants rigorous monitoring, testing, reporting and enforceable measures, including "things that are not easy for the company to just pay to get rid of."

What the permit covers:
- Emissions from a furnace, a thermal oxidizer, high and low pressure flares, diesel generators, diesel firewater pumps and vents ([Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/udpate-public-comment-period-open-for-woodfibre-lng-air-emissions-application-12855424)).
- Woodfibre says its modelling shows air pollution in nearby communities staying below B.C. air quality objectives, and it must keep monitoring air at the site and around it (same story).
- The application runs about 4,149 pages ([My Sea to Sky](https://myseatosky.org/news/updates/woodfibre-lngs-toxic-air-pollution-permit/)).
- Woodfibre is still getting permits for its original design even though it has announced an expansion ([The Narwhal](https://thenarwhal.ca/bc-woodfibre-lng-squamish-air-quality-data/)).
- For comparison, the regulator says LNG Canada has had repeated flaring that did not meet its permit, though with no measurable effect on local air quality ([The Narwhal](https://thenarwhal.ca/bc-woodfibre-lng-squamish-air-quality-data/)).

## How to comment on the permit
- Email comments to Woodfibre LNG, with a copy to the BC Energy Regulator ([Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/udpate-public-comment-period-open-for-woodfibre-lng-air-emissions-application-12855424)).
- Woodfibre applied on October 29, opening a 30 day comment window ([The Narwhal](https://thenarwhal.ca/bc-woodfibre-lng-squamish-air-quality-data/)). By our arithmetic, 30 days from October 29 is November 28, but [My Sea to Sky](https://myseatosky.org/news/updates/woodfibre-lngs-toxic-air-pollution-permit/) gives the deadline as November 27. Aim for November 27 and confirm with the BC Energy Regulator.
- The regulator makes the decision. When it will decide is not known.
- To write to your trustees, their emails are on the [school district's trustees page](https://www.sd48seatosky.org/apps/pages/trustees).

[[bars window]]
## Key dates
- October 17: trustees elected for four year terms ([SD48](https://www.sd48seatosky.org/apps/pages/trusteeelections2026)).
- October 29: Woodfibre applies for its air permit ([The Narwhal](https://thenarwhal.ca/bc-woodfibre-lng-squamish-air-quality-data/)).
- November 18: trustees take their oaths and hold their first regular meeting.
- November 27: comment deadline given by [My Sea to Sky](https://myseatosky.org/news/updates/woodfibre-lngs-toxic-air-pollution-permit/). A full 30 days from filing would be November 28, so aim for the 27th and confirm with the regulator.
- November 30: assistant superintendent Paul Lorette retires.
- 2027: the District of Squamish expects the Woodfibre project to be finished ([District of Squamish](https://squamish.ca/projects-plans-and-initiatives/projects-in-our-community/woodfibre-liquefied-natural-gas-and-fortisbceagle-mountain-pipeline/woodfibre-lng-project/)).
- End of 2027 or early 2028: when the company hopes for first cargoes ([Resourceworks](https://resourceworks.com/snapshot-woodfibre-lng/)).

## Still unknown
- When the parent letter will go out, or when the next board meeting is.
- Whether the provincial age rules apply on school grounds, which may not count as a highway.
- Which bikes count as light or standard, in plain terms.
- Which schools stored e-bikes, and how many students ride them.
- We could not find a written school district policy on e-bikes or e-bike storage.
- Whether the regulator must respond to comments.
- Whether the board's Woodfibre letter will arrive before the deadline.

## Other business
- Trustees took their oaths of office on November 18, before the meeting.
- April Lowe stays on as board chair, and Whistler's Cynthia Higgins stays as vice chair.
- It was the last board meeting for Paul Lorette. Lowe thanked him on behalf of the board and said he was once her principal.

The full meeting is on the school district's YouTube channel.

- Wellbeing

stories.head: Farm or animals hit by the floods? There's a coordinator you can call
stories.dek: Farmers, ranchers and livestock owners hurt by the floods can get help with emergency needs for their animals and farms. The Squamish-Lillooet Regional District's Agricultural Coordinator is at 604-384-7329. The regional district also encourages producers to register for a Premises ID and to record their flood damage and losses.
gist: Farmers, ranchers and livestock owners hurt by the floods can call the regional district's Agricultural Coordinator at 604-384-7329.
The coordinator helps arrange emergency needs for livestock, other animals and farm operations.
The regional district asks producers to register for a Premises ID.
Keeping a record of damage to buildings, equipment, crops and livestock can support an insurance claim or a request for recovery help.
stories.take: If the floods hit your farm or animals, call the Agricultural Coordinator at 604-384-7329 and start keeping a record of your damage and losses.
stories.body:
[[glance]]

## Who can help

The Squamish-Lillooet Regional District has an Agricultural Coordinator for people hurt by the recent floods who work with farms or animals: farmers, ranchers and livestock owners, whom the regional district calls producers.

The coordinator can help them coordinate livestock, animal and other agriculture-related emergency needs.

You can reach the Agricultural Coordinator at 604-384-7329. The release does not list hours for the line.

## Two steps to take now

The regional district encourages producers to do two things:

- Register for a Premises ID.
- Document damage and losses.

When you document, keep a record of damage and losses to your:

- Buildings
- Equipment
- Crops
- Livestock

These records can support insurance claims or requests for recovery assistance.

## What the release does not say

The release does not explain what a Premises ID is or how to register for one, and it gives no separate contact for registering. Producers with questions could ask the coordinator. The release also does not say what kinds of recovery assistance may be offered.

## More from us

- Before heading out to check on fields or animals near the water, see current river levels, weather and Highway 99 conditions on our [today page](/today/).
- Related coverage is on our [flood protection page](/issues/flood-protection/).

Source: [Squamish-Lillooet Regional District news release](https://e1.envoke.com/ext/click/go/72b42360f6f117b691464136292515ef/d5567e947c4a99bfce76b00dd2250505/6cd9fbfbbbbeeabe00dc6e15657d2f75)
stories.social:
Flooding hit your farm, livestock or crops?

The regional district has an Agricultural Coordinator who can help with emergency needs for farms and animals. Producers are encouraged to register for a Premises ID (ask the coordinator how) and to keep a record of all damage for insurance or recovery help. Number to save: 604-384-7329.

## What is happening

A November 20 [news release](https://e1.envoke.com/ext/click/go/72b42360f6f117b691464136292515ef/afd176d0d767dcbe6286b00dd224baaa/6cd9fbfbbbbeeabe00dc6e15657d2f75) says road damage continues to affect access in the Squamish Valley, which is Electoral Area D. - Who counts as local traffic.

## When and where

The rules start Tuesday, December 1. These are the 18 streets as currently listed on the District's [winter parking page](https://squamish.ca/transportation-parking-and-mobility/parking/winter-parking/) and reported by the [Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/squamish-todayjan-6-heres-what-you-need-to-know-before-you-head-out-8348303) (our count):

- Hemlock Avenue, Chestnut Avenue and Fir Street
- Third, Fourth, Fifth and Sixth Avenues
- Eaglewind Boulevard, Edgewater Drive and Edgewater Crescent
- No Name Road, Brothers Place and Britannia Avenue
- Harris Road, Hope Road, Diamond Road and Diamond Head Road
- Glacier View Drive
- Third Avenue: east side from Pemberton Avenue to Winnipeg Street, west side from Pemberton Avenue to Vancouver Street.

The District says No Parking applies on the side shown by signs, so check the signs and the interactive map. It reviews the list each season.

The District's notice says the rules run until March 1, 2026, a date that has already passed. The District's winter parking page gives the season as December 1 to March 1 with no year, and the District has not confirmed the year.

## The ticket and towing

The ticket is for "impeding snow removal," meaning parking that blocks snow clearing. Under [Bylaw 2418](https://squamish.civicweb.net/document/200801/), the District's ticket bylaw:

- The fine is $250.
- It drops to $200 if paid within 14 days.
- It rises to $300 if paid after 28 days.
- This ticket can't be reduced through a compliance agreement.

[[bars fine]]
The District may tow vehicles when necessary and [without notice](https://squamish.ca/transportation-parking-and-mobility/parking/parking-regulations/). When parking affects public safety, your car may be impounded right away.

## How the rules came about

- December 2021 and January 2022: snow and ice storms. Cars [parked on both sides](https://squamish.ca/transportation-parking-and-mobility/parking/winter-parking/) kept plows out.
- October 18, 2022: [Bylaw 2932](https://squamish.civicweb.net/document/200801/) adds the $250 fine. A companion change, Bylaw 2930, adds the no parking rule to the [Traffic Bylaw](https://squamish.civicweb.net/document/200803/).
- December 2022: rules [start](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2022/12/13/winter-parking-restrictions-now-in-effect-in-squamish/), with officers focused on education and warnings.
- 2023 to 2024: the District calls the program a success and [adds streets](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/winter-parking-restrictions-to-hit-some-squamish-streets-on-dec-1-7880343).
- December 1, 2026: this season begins.

The District has [three snow plow trucks](https://squamish.ca/transportation-parking-and-mobility/road-maintenance-and-snow-clearing/snow-and-ice-control/snow-clearing-faq/) plus a machine for trails, sidewalks and school routes. First priority goes to main roads and major connecting roads, bus routes, police, fire and ambulance stations, hills and safe routes to school. Residential streets come third.

## What you can do

- Check your street at [squamish.ca/winter-parking](https://squamish.ca/winter-parking) before December 1.
- Do not park within 1.5 metres of a driveway.
- Use your garage or driveway, and pile shovelled snow to the right of your driveway, facing the road, as the [District advises](https://squamish.ca/transportation-parking-and-mobility/road-maintenance-and-snow-clearing/snow-and-ice-control/).
- Clear the sidewalk next to your property. [Owners and occupiers must](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/news/new-parking-restrictions-introduced-to-improve-snow-and-ice-clearing/); that ticket is $100, or $90 early and $110 late, under Bylaw 2418.

[[bars sidewalk]]
## What we don't know yet

- The correct end year
- How strictly the rules will be enforced this winter
- The cost of a tow and which company tows
- Where towed cars are taken
- How to dispute a ticket
- How many tickets and tows since 2022
- Whether any streets changed for 2026 to 2027

For these answers, ask the District's bylaw staff.

More: our [parking issue page](/issues/parking/), and [Today in Squamish](/today/) for today's local conditions. Source: [District of Squamish E-News](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/enews-archives/), November 20, 2026.

stories.dek: If you pay the District of Squamish for a rec program, a business licence, filming or a development application, some fees may change on January 2, 2027. The District's notice does not list the new amounts.
gist: On January 2, 2027, some District of Squamish fees change, in areas including business licences, filming, development, and parks and recreation.
The District's notice does not say which fees go up or down, or by how much.
To see the full list, search the District of Squamish website for Amendment Bylaw No. 3249, 2026.
That bylaw updates the District's Fees and Charges Bylaw No. 3185, 2025, so it is worth checking before you pay a fee in the new year.

glance.v: Old or new fee: not stated

stories.take: Before you pay a District fee on or after January 2, 2027, look up Amendment Bylaw No. 3249, 2026 on the District of Squamish website to see the new amount.
stories.body:
[[glance]]

## What is changing

An amendment to the District's Fees and Charges Bylaw (No. 3185, 2025) takes effect January 2, 2027. It affects some of the fees the District of Squamish charges for its applications, services and programs.

The District says the change affects fees in areas including:

- Business licensing (see our [jobs and economy](/issues/jobs-and-economy/) page)
- Filming
- Development (see our [growth and development](/issues/growth-and-development/) page)
- Parks and recreation (see our [Brennan Park and recreation](/issues/brennan-park-and-recreation/) page)

The amendment is called Amendment Bylaw No. 3249, 2026.

## Timeline

- November 20, 2026: the District announces the change in its E-News
- January 2, 2027: the new fees take effect

That is 43 days between the notice and the start date (our count).

## What we don't know yet

The District's notice leaves several questions open:

- Which fees go up, which go down, and which stay the same
- How much any single fee changes
- Whether a registration or application made before January 2 pays the old fee or the new one

We have not yet seen the new amounts, so this story does not compare old and new fees.

## How to see the full list

The notice points residents to the full bylaw for the complete list of fees, but it does not include a direct link. To find it, search the District of Squamish website for this exact title:

- District of Squamish Fees and Charges Bylaw No. 3185, 2025, Amendment Bylaw No. 3249, 2026

If you plan to pay the District for something early in 2027, it may help to check the bylaw first.

The notice was posted in the District's [E-News](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/enews-archives/) on November 20, 2026.

stories.head: Mayor's motion to freeze 2027 tax revenue would need $6.3M in savings
stories.dek: Holding 2027 property tax revenue at the 2026 level would mean finding $6.3 million in savings while keeping services. Council considers Mayor Sean Easton's motion on Tuesday, December 1. You can say what you would invest more or less in at LetsTalkSquamish.ca.
gist: Council will decide whether to plan a 2027 budget that collects no more property tax money in total than in 2026.
A flat total is for the whole District, so your own bill can still change with your property's assessed value.
Staff say $3.6 million of the $6.3 million planned increase is already committed, and they have not named which jobs or services could change.
Council considers the motion on Tuesday, December 1, and you can share what you would spend more or less on at LetsTalkSquamish.ca.

glance.v: Service cuts, jobs, reserves, other revenue

savings.title: The $6.3 million increase in the draft 2027 budget, in millions of dollars
savings.note: Squamish Chief, November 19, 2026; the amount not already committed is our arithmetic

increase.title: Property tax increase, in percent
increase.note: 2026 increase and 10 year plan figure: Squamish Chief, January 2026. Staff draft: Squamish Voters property taxes page, November 2026. Motion: Squamish Reporter, November 16, 2026. The motion is about the District's total revenue; individual bills can still change.

home.title: Increase for the average home, in dollars
home.note: 2026: Squamish Chief, January 2026. 2027 staff draft as of November 9: Squamish Voters property taxes page.

stories.take: Budget feedback is open now at LetsTalkSquamish.ca with no deadline posted, and council considers the motion on Tuesday, December 1.
stories.body:
[[glance]]

## What the motion would do

On Tuesday, December 1, council will consider a motion for a 2027 budget with no increase in property tax revenue over 2026. The District says that would mean finding $6.3 million in savings while still delivering municipal services. The notice of motion came to council on November 17 and is scheduled for December 1 unless council decides otherwise ([Squamish Reporter](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2026/11/16/squamish-mayor-property-tax-revenue-2027/)).

The motion is about the District's total revenue. Changes in assessed values can still move individual bills.

The $6.3 million is the increase already built into staff's draft 2027 budget. Staff say $3.6 million of it is already committed or money the District has to spend ([Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/squamish-council-previews-debate-over-mayors-proposal-to-scrap-2027-budget-13035079)). By our arithmetic, at most about $2.7 million of the planned increase is open to change. So at least $3.6 million would have to come from existing services, positions, reserves or other revenue.

[[bars savings]]
## What the motion asks for

According to [the Squamish Reporter](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2026/11/16/squamish-mayor-property-tax-revenue-2027/):

- Staff, through the chief administrative officer, would prepare a revised draft 2027 budget with no increase in municipal property tax revenue.
- Services must be at least as accessible, available, timely and effective as in 2026.
- The District could not use more contractors to replace work its own employees normally do.
- The chief administrative officer would lead a review to find savings. The budget would show the effects on staffing, services, reserves, capital projects, debt, and fees.

The motion comes from [Mayor Sean Easton](/council/sean-easton/), who [promised during the campaign](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/mayor-sean-easton-moves-to-restart-squamish-budget-process-13013416) to freeze property taxes for 2027. He won on October 17 with 3,681 votes to Jenna Stoner's 3,506 ([District of Squamish](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/council/election/)). The new council decides: the mayor and Councillors [Eric Andersen](/council/eric-andersen/), [Janice DesJardins](/council/janice-desjardins/), [Sarah Ellis](/council/sarah-ellis/), [Luc Perreault](/council/luc-perreault/), [Laura Prosko](/council/laura-prosko/) and [Shaun Veltkamp](/council/shaun-veltkamp/).

## What staff told council

According to [the Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/squamish-council-previews-debate-over-mayors-proposal-to-scrap-2027-budget-13035079), staff listed four ways to find savings: service cuts, cutting positions, drawing on reserves and raising other revenues. B.C. municipalities must by law adopt a balanced budget.

- Tax funded special projects in 2027 total about $400,000, including the first year of the Official Community Plan update and the cost of hiring a chief administrative officer.
- Julie Wengi, general manager of corporate services, said reviews like this are not usually done just to cut a budget, and they take time and resources.
- Councillor Prosko asked staff to bring back two options: no increase, and a modest increase.

## What's in the budget

- In September, staff asked for $580,000 for 2027 for bylaw enforcement, BC Housing temporary housing support and a community safety plan, about 1.1% or $35 for the average home ([Squamish Reporter](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2026/09/27/squamish-budget-proposes-580000-for-encampment-response/)).
- The 10 year capital plan is $357 million through 2036 ([Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/squamish-municipal-budget-2027-heres-what-is-in-the-capital-plan-12894020)).
- About $58.7 million in transportation projects have no confirmed funding ([Squamish Reporter](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2026/11/03/squamish-transportation-projects-58-million-unfunded/)).
- Utility rates and curbside collection fees are also set to rise in 2027, separate from property tax revenue ([Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/squamish-2027-budget-process-council-works-to-save-taxpayers-a-few-bucks-on-totes-12827374)).

## The numbers and what is unknown

As of November 9, staff's draft started at a 10.4% increase, about $342 for the average home ([our property taxes page](/issues/property-taxes/)). The 2026 increase was 12.8% ($6.4 million), about $382. The District's first 10 year plan, adopted January 13, 2026, had projected 13% for 2027 ([Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/update-tough-budget-squamish-council-adopts-first-decade-long-financial-plan-11710524)).

[[bars increase]]
[[bars home]]
The 2026 general property tax requirement was $56.1 million. Total municipal tax revenue reached $61.9 million after more tax than expected came in from Woodfibre LNG properties and went to capital reserves ([Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/squamish-council-amends-10-year-financial-plan-boosts-reserves-with-woodfibre-lng-tax-windfall-12189221)).

Still unknown:

- Which positions or services could be cut.
- Whether tax from new construction counts toward the flat total.
- What a flat total means for each household's bill, including the school and regional district amounts on the same bill.
- How $6.3 million, about 11% of $56.1 million by our arithmetic, squares with the 10.4% draft.
- A feedback deadline, or when the plan will be adopted.

## How to take part

- Give feedback at [Let's Talk Budget 2027](https://letstalksquamish.ca/budget-2027). The review runs through December.
- A Budget Information Night is listed for November, date to be confirmed.
- Council meets Tuesday, December 1 in Council Chambers, Municipal Hall, 37955 Second Avenue ([our meeting page](/meetings/2026-12-01-regular/)).
- Watch live: [District of Squamish on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/@DistrictofSquamish/streams)
- Vote before council does at [Have your say](/have-your-say/)
- Source: [District of Squamish E-News](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/enews-archives/)
