stories.head: Squamish Nation fills an empty Council seat without a vote. Here's how
stories.dek: No new vote was needed: Roger Lewis, the runner-up in the 2025 Squamish Nation election, takes the Council seat Councillor Sinámḵin, Jody Broomfield, left this month. The logger from Ch’iyáḵmesh serves until 2029. He still has to sign his oath, and the Nation says ceremony details are coming.
gist: Roger Lewis, a logger and father of four, has been named to the Squamish Nation Council.
He fills the seat Jody Broomfield left on November 4, because Nation rules give an empty seat to the top candidate who just missed out last election.
He serves until the term ends in 2029, and the date of his oath signing ceremony has not been shared yet.
If the same kind of seat opens again this term, it could go to a vote just for that seat.

seats.title: Squamish Nation Council seats over time
seats.note: Sources: Khelsilem's Substack (Oct. 2025) for before 2017; Squamish Chief (Oct. 2025) for 2017 onward.

stories.take: Roger Lewis joins Squamish Nation Council for the rest of the 2025 to 2029 term once he signs his oath, and questions about the process can go to electoralcommission@squamish.net.
stories.body:
[[glance]]

This is the Squamish Nation's Council, not the District of Squamish council.

## How he got the seat

No new vote was held. The Nation's Election and Referendum Law says the runner-up from the last general election can take an empty seat, if that person is still eligible and accepts. The 2025 results named Roger Lewis as the runner-up. He is still eligible and has accepted the seat for the rest of the 2025 to 2029 term.

The law was [approved by members on Dec. 6, 2018](https://www.squamish.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Electoral-Commission-Statement-January-19-2024.pdf), and the Nation's website posts both the [2018 text](https://www.squamish.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/SN-Election-and-Referendum-Law-2018.pdf) and a [June 2025 version](https://www.squamish.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Election-and-Referendum-Law-June-2025.pdf). The 2018 text defines the runner-up as the candidate with the most votes who was not elected, and gives that person 30 days after being told to take a first vacancy. Under the June 2025 version, a by-election is used when the runner-up does not take the seat or for a second vacancy in the same office between regular elections.

The Electoral Commission, an independent group of seven members, guided Chairperson and Council through the process. A [January 2024 Electoral Commission statement](https://www.squamish.net/ec-statement/) says Deborah Baker, runner-up in the previous election, filled a vacant seat after giving notarized proof of eligibility.

Councillor Sinámḵin, Jody Broomfield, [resigned on November 4](https://squamish.net/regarding-councillor-sinam%E1%B8%B5in-jody-broomfield), effective right away, for personal and medical reasons. The Nation's [results page](https://www.squamish.net/governance/general-election/) lists Broomfield with 601 votes in 2025. We did not find Lewis's total.

## Who he is

- Comes from the village of Ch’iyáḵmesh
- Parents Paul and Wendy Lewis; grandparents the late Jacob Lewis and Betty (nee Billy); great grandfathers Louie Lewis and Dominic Charlie
- A father of four and, in the Nation's words, a fifth generation logger
- Most recently a superintendent with Nch’ḵay̓ Development Corporation, which a [2024 Resource Works article](https://resourceworks.com/red-ink-flags-for-forestry/) called the Nation's economic arm; it said he had logged for 25 years
- The Squamish Chief has [covered him patrolling the Squamish Valley](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/bracing-for-the-summer-season-in-the-squamish-valley-8629543), including after a human caused wildfire on the Squamish River Forest Service Road

An [op-ed](https://thefutureeconomy.ca/op-eds/indigenous-forestry-john-desjarlais-indigenous-resource-network/) calls him a seventh generation forester, which differs from the Nation's wording.

## The council he joins

The 2025 election was held Sept. 28, 2025. Chairperson Wilson Williams was acclaimed, replacing Khelsilem, who did not run. Two councillors were re-elected and 13 new general councillors were elected, [the Squamish Chief reported](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/squamish-nation-elects-new-council-chairperson-and-band-manager-11281998). Council grew from eight seats to 16 that year, ending the dedicated North Shore, Squamish Valley and outside region seats. The Squamish Chief says the 16 reflects the 16 families that amalgamated in 1923.

[[bars seats]]
The change came through a 2025 referendum; about 3,300 members were [eligible to vote](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/referendum-could-reshape-squamish-nation-council-structure-10731328). Khelsilem [wrote](https://khelsilem.substack.com/p/squamish-nation-enters-new-era-of) that the Nation had 16 seats before cutting back in 2017, and that the return to 16 passed "by the slimmest of margins."

Separately, the Squamish Chief [reported on August 19, 2026](https://www.squamishchief.com/in-the-community/squamish-nation-councillors-suspended-under-pending-investigation-12681035) that two councillors were suspended after an alleged incident on June 28, 2026. We found no later update.

## What comes next

- An oath signing ceremony to formally mark his appointment, with date and place still to be shared
- Questions about the process: electoralcommission@squamish.net
- Still not public: his 2025 vote count, whether he stays at Nch’ḵay̓, and whether the ceremony is open to members

Chairperson Sxwíxwtn Wilson Williams welcomed him: "Roger carries a strong passion, innovation, and versatility to his leadership style, and we look forward to continuing our work serving the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh (Squamish) People together."

Read the [Squamish Nation announcement](https://www.squamish.net/new-councillor-announcement/).
stories.social:
Roger Lewis is the newest Squamish Nation councillor, and no new vote put him there. Nation rules give a seat that opens between elections to the runner-up from the last election.

He fills the seat Jody Broomfield left on November 4 and serves until 2029. Because the runner-up filled this first vacancy, a second one this term could go to a by-election, a vote just for that seat.

## Who fills in for the mayor

Council is set to vote on who serves as acting mayor for the next two months. The acting mayor is the councillor who fills in when the mayor is away.

The agenda asks council to change its acting mayor list for December 1, 2026, to January 31, 2027, so it reads:

- December 2026: [Councillor Andersen](/council/eric-andersen/)
- January 2027: [Councillor Ellis](/council/sarah-ellis/)

The agenda describes this as an amendment to the existing appointments. It does not say who held these months before.

## The closed part

Most of this short morning meeting is set to happen in private. Right after adopting the agenda, council will vote to close the meeting to the public under section 90(1)(a), (g) and (i) of the Community Charter, the provincial law for municipalities. The agenda lists three reasons:

- information about a person who holds or is being considered for a staff or appointed position with the District
- a legal case or possible lawsuit affecting the District
- advice from the District's lawyers that is kept private by law

The agenda gives no more detail on any of these matters. The acting mayor vote is listed after the motion to close, and the agenda does not say when council returns to open session. People watching live from 9 a.m. should know the vote has no set time.

stories.head: Did Squamish hit its first year housing target? Council sees it Nov 24
stories.dek: Did Squamish finish the 160 homes the Province required in the first year of its order for 1,069 homes by 2030? Council receives the full year report on Tuesday, November 24, at 4:30 p.m. at Municipal Hall. It is a council workshop with no final votes.
gist: The Province has ordered Squamish to have at least 1,069 new homes finished and lived in over the five years ending August 2030.
By the end of February, halfway through the first year, 153 homes were done against a first year minimum of 160.
The full first year count goes to council on Tuesday, November 24, and it is not yet known what the Province can do if a target is missed.
You can go to Municipal Hall, watch on the District's YouTube channel, or join by WebEx or phone from 4:30 p.m.

ramp.title: Finished homes required, by year of the order
ramp.note: Source: Squamish Reporter, September 2, 2025 and March 23, 2026. Years 2 to 4 combined is our arithmetic (1,069 minus 160 minus 299). Year 2 to 4 split not published.

stories.take: Tuesday's report shows whether Squamish finished the 160 homes the Province required for Year 1; it is the only public item, 4:30 to 5:30 p.m.
stories.body:
[[glance]]

## What council will look at

On Tuesday, November 24, council will receive the second progress report on the housing target the Province set for Squamish under the Housing Supply Act. The first report covered only six months, so this is the first to cover a full year: September 1, 2025 to August 31, 2026, Year 1 of the order. It is posted with the [agenda](https://squamish.civicweb.net/document/272267/), on pages 3 to 17. Jessie Fletcher, the District's Director of Community Development, presents it. The agenda sets aside 4:30 p.m. to 5:30 p.m.

Staff ask council only to receive the report. This is a Committee of the Whole, a council workshop with no final votes. It is not yet known what the Province can do if a target is missed; the sources we found do not say.

After the housing report, council plans to close the meeting under section 90 of the Community Charter. It will talk with staff about District goals, measures and progress reports for the annual municipal report.

## How Squamish did at the halfway mark

The first report, received by council on [March 24, 2026](https://squamish.civicweb.net/document/263693/), covered September 1, 2025 to February 28, 2026. It showed 153 finished homes, close to the full year minimum of 160 in half the time. Staff expected Squamish to pass the Year 1 target ([Squamish Reporter](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2026/03/23/squamish-meets-provincial-housing-pace-but-falls-short-on-federal-targets/)). By our arithmetic, that left 7 more homes needed in the second half of Year 1.

[[bars halfway]]
## What the order requires

The Province ordered Squamish to have at least 1,069 new homes finished over five years, from September 1, 2025 to August 31, 2030 ([Squamish Reporter](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2025/09/02/minister-links-squamish-housing-order-to-infrastructure-funding/)). By our arithmetic, that averages about 214 homes a year. Only finished homes that people move into count, not approvals ([Squamish Reporter](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2026/02/10/district-explores-ways-to-fast-track-housing-developments/)). The order is the Housing Minister's. Council only receives the reports ([Province of B.C.](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/housing-tenancy/local-governments-and-housing/housing-targets/orders)).

- Year 1 minimum: 160 homes. The targets rise each year, and Year 5 alone needs 299 ([Squamish Reporter](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2026/03/23/squamish-meets-provincial-housing-pace-but-falls-short-on-federal-targets/)). That leaves 610 for Years 2 to 4 combined, by our arithmetic.

[[bars ramp]]
- 1,069 is 75% of the Province's estimate of Squamish's need, 1,425 homes ([Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/opinion/editorial-is-squamish-on-track-to-meet-new-provincial-housing-targets-11120977)).
- Housing Minister Christine Boyle wrote that Squamish "should strive to achieve 100 per cent" of that need ([Squamish Reporter](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2025/09/02/minister-links-squamish-housing-order-to-infrastructure-funding/)).
- The Province suggested a mix by size, but says it is not binding: 615 studios or one bedroom homes, 195 two bedroom homes and 257 with three or more bedrooms ([Squamish Reporter](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2025/09/02/minister-links-squamish-housing-order-to-infrastructure-funding/)).
- Squamish is in Group 4 of the [provincial orders](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/housing-tenancy/local-governments-and-housing/housing-targets/orders), with places like Burnaby, Coquitlam, Richmond and Vernon. The 10 Group 4 towns and cities are expected to deliver 38,930 homes by 2030 ([Squamish Reporter](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2025/08/25/province-sets-five-year-housing-goal-for-squamish/)).
- The District's 2023 Housing Needs Assessment said Squamish needs 6,840 new homes by 2031, a separate estimate over a different time frame ([District of Squamish](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/news/squamish-added-to-housing-targets-program/)).

[[bars needs]]
## Other housing targets

- The District approved building permits for 434 homes in 2025, leaving it 286 units behind its federal housing targets ([Squamish Reporter, March 2026](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2026/03/23/squamish-meets-provincial-housing-pace-but-falls-short-on-federal-targets/)). These federal figures count building permits; the provincial order counts finished, occupied homes.
- In February 2026, Squamish was 276 units short of its target under the federal Housing Accelerator Fund, and 711 short of the target in its own Housing Needs Report. Staff proposed five changes to speed up approvals ([Squamish Reporter, February 2026](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2026/02/10/district-explores-ways-to-fast-track-housing-developments/)).
- Ottawa committed $7 million to Squamish through that fund ([District of Squamish](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/news/squamish-added-to-housing-targets-program/)). At its second annual report to the fund, Squamish had reached 69% of its Year 2 forecast and 42% of its three year target of 1,539 units, and received a third payment of $1,751,973.58 ([Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation](https://assets.cmhc-schl.gc.ca/sites/cmhc/professional/project-funding-and-mortgage-financing/funding-programs/all-funding-programs/housing-accelerator-fund/action-plan-summaries/haf-action-plan-summaries-squamish-en.pdf)).
- Housing Squamish aims to have 300 affordable homes underway by 2029 ([Squamish Reporter](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2025/11/24/housing-squamish-says-it-turned-1-5m-into-nearly-11m-for-affordable-homes/)).

## What is still unknown

We could not open the 15 page report, so we cannot yet say whether Squamish met 160. We also could not find the separate targets for Years 2 to 4.

## How to take part

- When: Tuesday, November 24, 2026, 4:30 p.m. (housing report 4:30 to 5:30 p.m.)
- Where: Council Chambers, Municipal Hall, 37955 Second Avenue, Squamish
- Open to the public for the housing report, before the meeting closes
- The agenda does not say whether the public can speak on this item
- Watch live on the District's YouTube channel; recorded for the District website
- Join online by WebEx: [participating in meetings](https://squamish.civicweb.net/Portal/227149/ParticipatinginMeetings/)
- Join by phone: call 1-604-449-3026, access code 2773 519 7595
- Agenda: [November 24 agenda](https://squamish.civicweb.net/document/272267/)
- Our page: [Committee of the Whole, November 24](/meetings/2026-11-24-cow/)

More on our [housing issue page](/issues/housing/) and [growth and development page](/issues/growth-and-development/).

stories.take: Anyone visiting the Library can watch Rose Williams weave and talk with her about her work, mostly on Saturdays between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m.
stories.body:
[[glance]]

## Where and when

- Place: Squamish Public Library, 37907 Second Avenue
- Days: mostly Saturdays, over the coming months
- Hours: Saturdays 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. ([Library hours](https://squamishlibrary.ca/news/expanded-library-hours/))
- Who can come: anyone visiting the Library is welcome to watch and talk with Williams about her work
- Exact dates have not been posted. Check the [Library website](https://www.squamishlibrary.ca/) or ask Library staff before you go.

## How it came about

The Library [put out a call on April 9, 2026](https://squamishlibrary.ca/news/call-for-s%E1%B8%B5wx%CC%B1wu7mesh-uxwumixw-artists/) asking Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish Nation) artists to propose a permanent indoor artwork recognizing that the Library sits on the Nation's traditional, ancestral and unceded territory. The idea grew out of a reconciliation statement written by the Library board and endorsed by Squamish Valley Elders, [the Squamish Chief reported](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/honouring-reconciliation-squamish-library-calls-for-nation-artists-12160245). Ideally the artwork would show the statement's words; the Library has not said whether this weaving will.

- Proposals were due May 22, 2026.
- Library board trustees and staff reviewed them, and the final choice needed the support of Squamish Nation Elders.
- The winner was to be named the week of June 22, 2026.
- Installation was first planned for fall 2026. The new notice says the weaving will take the coming months.

[[bars timeline]]
The Library has not publicly said whether Williams was picked through this call, or how many artists applied.

## Who pays

The call offered $10,000 to make and install the work, [the Squamish Chief reported (via the Penticton Herald)](https://www.pentictonherald.ca/spare_news/article_5910cb68-afea-51e3-bb08-e3ba137ac82e.html). Part of the money comes from a [Province of B.C. library enhancement grant](https://squamishlibrary.ca/news/call-for-s%E1%B8%B5wx%CC%B1wu7mesh-uxwumixw-artists/), and the board added a [new 2026 budget line](https://squamishlibrary.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Board-Meeting-Minutes-April-2026.pdf) for a reconciliation project that includes an art installation. The split has not been made public. For scale, the Library's total provincial grants were [$97,143.48 in 2024](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/residents/sports-and-recreation/arts-culture/public-libraries/funding/2024_public_libraries_provincial_grants_allocations.pdf).

[[bars money]]
In June 2025 the Province added [another $1.25 million in one time Library Enhancement Grants](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/residents/sports-and-recreation/arts-culture/public-libraries/funding/2025_public_libraries_provincial_grants_allocations.pdf) for B.C. libraries. The Library has not said which year's enhancement grant it used.

## About the weaver

Williams learned cedar weaving from Sesemiya Tracy Williams, and wool weaving from Chepximiya Siyam Chief Janice George and Skwetsimeltxw Willard "Buddy" Joseph, [according to Simon Fraser University](https://www.sfu.ca/annieross/research-mentors/williams.html). Her pieces are in private collections and museum exhibits. She has [woven in wool since 2006 and now works mainly in wool](https://www.selenakearney.com/aweaversvoice/project-six-6f87e-2eyxx). An [earlier North Shore News profile](https://www.nsnews.com/living/squamish-weaver-shares-her-skills-2991908) said she worked with the Squamish Nation Education Department and was interested in mountain goat wool and old spinning and dyeing methods. The Library has not said what materials she will use.

George and Joseph, her wool weaving teachers, are central to the craft's comeback. Traditional weaving had almost disappeared in the Squamish Nation after colonization, and the two [started a major revival in the early 2000s](http://www.sfu.ca/archive-sfunews/news/story_03190901.shtml). They [co-founded L'hen Awtxw Weaving House](https://ecuad.ca/chepximiya-siyam-chief-janice-george-on-the-life-giving-power-of-culture/) to teach Coast Salish wool weaving.

## Nation art at the Library

- 2021: Siobhan Joseph's "Why the Salmon Come to Squamish Waters" wraps the north and east windows ([Library](https://squamishlibrary.ca/art-at-the-library/)), paid for by a Squamish Arts Council grant and District of Squamish capital funding ([North Shore News](https://www.nsnews.com/local-news/library-calls-for-squamish-nation-artists-for-unique-window-project-3149161)).
- Master carver X̱walacktun carved two eagles on the Community Meeting Room doors; in 1999 Squamish Nation Elders approved the room's name in the Squamish language ([Art at the Library](https://squamishlibrary.ca/art-at-the-library/)).
- 2021: Tsawaysia Spukwus (Alice Guss) taught [free wool weaving workshops](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2021/05/28/free-wool-weaving-drum-making-workshops-by-alice-guss-at-library/) at the Library.

For comparison, North Vancouver City Library has had [two Coast Salish weavings on display since 2023](https://www.nvcl.ca/public-art).

Still unknown: the size, design, title, where it will hang and when it will be done.

stories.head: Kayaker, 29, dies on Cheakamus River; fourth water death in four days
stories.dek: A Squamish woman, 29, died after her kayak capsized on the Cheakamus River on Sunday, November 15. Police say it is the fourth death on Squamish waterways in four days, after a boat flipped on the Squamish River on November 12. They ask anyone on or near the water to plan ahead and wear a life jacket.
gist: A woman from Squamish, 29, died after her kayak tipped over in the Cheakamus River just north of town on November 15.
Police say she is the fourth person to die on Squamish waters in four days, after three people died when a boat flipped on November 12.
A heavy rainstorm pushed the Squamish River to its highest flow on record for November 12, and police say they have seen very high water and lots of debris.
Police ask people to plan trips, check weather and tides, wear life jackets and carry cold water safety gear.

stories.take: Police ask anyone heading on or near the water to plan the trip, check forecasts and tides, and wear an appropriate life jacket.
stories.body:
[[glance]]

A Squamish woman, 29, died Sunday, November 15, after her kayak capsized on the Cheakamus River. Police say it is the fourth death on Squamish waterways in four days.

Police ask people to take extensive caution on and around rivers, lakes and the ocean: plan the trip, check weather forecasts and tides, bring cold water safety gear, wear an appropriate life jacket and be ready for emergencies. For current river and weather conditions, see our [today page](/today/).

## What happened

At about 2:30 p.m. on November 15, BC Ambulance asked Squamish RCMP for help with two kayakers who had capsized in the Cheakamus River, just north of Squamish.

The two were part of a larger group of [white water kayakers](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/squamish-kayaker-dies-on-cheakamus-river-13021813). They had gone ahead of the others when they capsized. The group found one of them, [a man](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/kayaker-death-cheakamus-river-bc-9.7423570), safe. A woman was still missing, so Squamish Search and Rescue was called out. Search teams found her further downstream. Despite all efforts, she died at the scene.

"Our thoughts are with the woman's family and friends, and the first responders on scene," said Staff Sergeant Sascha Banks, Operations Commander of the Squamish RCMP Detachment.

## Fourth death in four days

The other three deaths came from one incident. On November 12, a boat with eight people aboard flipped on the flooded Squamish River near the 15900 block of Squamish Valley Road, and [three people died](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/three-of-our-friends-are-dead-survivor-recounts-squamish-river-boat-capsizing-13024486). A survivor [told the Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/three-of-our-friends-are-dead-survivor-recounts-squamish-river-boat-capsizing-13024486) the group had set out to check on farm animals and neighbours before the boat was swept against a log and flipped. RCMP are still investigating, and [investigators are trying to find out](https://globalnews.ca/news/12149734/2-people-dead-one-missing-boating-accident-squamish-valley/) why the boat was on the water in those conditions. The victims have not been publicly named in coverage.

## Timeline

- November 10 to 12: a heavy rainstorm dropped [159.5 mm of rain at Squamish Airport](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/squamish-flood-update-paradise-valley-shelter-advisory-ends-road-closures-remain-13010625).
- November 11: the [River Forecast Centre](https://bcrfc.env.gov.bc.ca/warnings/advisories/FWN_2026_11_11_1030_SC_VI_UPG.pdf) raised a flood warning for Howe Sound and the North Shore mountains.
- November 12: the Squamish River flow was [the highest ever recorded](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/stay-back-from-riverbanks-district-of-squamish-warns-of-erosion-after-flooding-13010625) at its gauge for that date. The [District said](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/news/flood-warning-issued-for-howe-sound-and-sea-to-sky/) the Cheakamus had peaked but was still well above normal. The boat flipped that afternoon.
- November 13: the third body was [recovered](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/three-of-our-friends-are-dead-survivor-recounts-squamish-river-boat-capsizing-13024486) after a search by Squamish Search and Rescue, RCMP Air Services and the RCMP Underwater Recovery Team. BC Hydro was [reducing spill](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/squamish-flood-update-paradise-valley-shelter-advisory-ends-road-closures-remain-13010625) (extra water released past the Cheakamus Dam). Squamish Valley Road [was closed northbound at the Cheakamus River Bridge](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/inside-slrd/news-notices/ongoing-flood-implications-squamish-valley) as of November 13; we found no newer update.
- November 15: the kayaker died on the Cheakamus River.
- November 16: a high streamflow advisory for Howe Sound, the North Shore mountains and the Sea to Sky was [lifted](https://lethbridgeherald.com/news/national-news/2026/11/16/swollen-b-c-rivers-claim-lives-as-boats-kayaks-capsize/). The flood warning had run from Wednesday to Friday.

[[bars rain]]
In a release dated November 18, police said they have seen incredibly high water levels and extensive debris, with flow rates rarely seen in recent memory. The District has asked people to [stay back from riverbanks](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/stay-back-from-riverbanks-district-of-squamish-warns-of-erosion-after-flooding-13010625) left unstable by erosion.

A similar storm in [November 2021](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/news/evacuation-alert-issued-for-paradise-valley-properties-in-areas-upstream-of-the-bailey-bridge/) led to a Paradise Valley evacuation alert and a Cheakamus Dam spill. BC Hydro must issue a Spill Notice when it releases more than 170 cubic metres per second.

## What we don't know

- How fast the Cheakamus was flowing on November 15, or whether the dam spill was still going on.
- Whether the kayakers wore life jackets, or why the boat was out on November 12.
- Whether the BC Coroners Service is looking into the deaths.
- Whether more rain is forecast, or when Squamish Valley Road will reopen.

## Safety help

BC AdventureSmart has paddling and water safety tips at [adventuresmart.ca](https://www.adventuresmart.ca/programs/paddlesmart/). Read the [RCMP news release](https://rcmp.ca/en/bc/squamish/news/2026/11/4358895).

stories.head: Squamish's first Legacy Award goes to Todd Pope. Here's why it was created
stories.dek: A nomination for Citizen of the Year after Todd Pope's death led the Squamish Chamber of Commerce to create a brand new award. His family accepted the first Squamish Legacy Award for him on Friday, November 13, at the Chamber's Business Excellence Awards at Capilano University.
gist: Todd Pope is the first person to get the new Squamish Legacy Award from the Squamish Chamber of Commerce.
He died in May at age 56, and a nomination for Citizen of the Year after his death led the Chamber to create the new award.
He moved to Squamish in 1993 and volunteered with trail, biking, skiing, race and police groups for years.
His family has asked for gifts in his memory to Easter Seals Camp Squamish.

life.title: Todd Pope in Squamish, 1993 to 2026 (years)
life.note: Sources: Squamish Funeral Chapel and North Shore News obituaries, Squamish Chief (2022). Years in Squamish is our arithmetic from his 1993 move to his death in 2026.

stories.take: Residents who want to honour Todd Pope can give to Easter Seals Camp Squamish in his memory.
stories.body:
[[glance]]

Todd Pope, a long-time Squamish volunteer who died in May, is the first person to receive the Squamish Chamber of Commerce's new Squamish Legacy Award. His wife and his son Jeremy accepted it on his behalf on Friday, November 13, at the Squamish Chamber Business Excellence Awards in the Library building at Capilano University in Squamish.

His family has asked for gifts in his memory to Easter Seals Camp Squamish. The [memorial page](https://www.eastersealsbcy.ca/get-involved/gift-in-memory/in-memory-of-todd-pope/) aims to raise $3,850, the cost of one camp experience. His daughter Hannah began attending the camp in 2019.

## Why a new award was made

Todd was nominated, after his death, for the Chamber's Bill Manson Citizen of the Year Award. That nomination inspired the Chamber to create the Squamish Legacy Award. It recognizes someone whose contributions have left a lasting mark on the community.

The Chamber says Todd volunteered his time, shared his talents and made a difference across countless local organizations and initiatives.

## Who Todd Pope was to Squamish

Todd was born December 4, 1969, and moved to Squamish in 1993, according to his [obituary](https://www.squamishfuneralchapel.com/obituaries/Todd-Frederick-Pope?obId=48443876). He is survived by his wife, daughter Hannah and son Jeremy. The obituary lists some of the groups he volunteered with:

- Test of Metal
- Squamish Trail Society
- Tourism Squamish
- Local triathlons
- Sea to Sky Nordics
- RCMP COPS and Auxiliary
- Squamish BMX and BMX Canada

His [LinkedIn profile](https://www.linkedin.com/in/popetodd/), which is self-reported, also lists RCMP auxiliary constable from 2002, Squamish Nordics Ski Club president and coach, and lead organizer of Test of Metal. An undated [Squamish Chief article](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/unhappy-trails-for-harvey-3338897) reports the District of Squamish hired him as a full-time trails coordinator at $26 an hour.

[[bars life]]
- 2022: had been Squamish BMX president for seven years, and was president of the BMX Canada Track Development Group, which owns 19 tracks across B.C. ([Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-sports/squamish-bmx-builds-back-even-better-5532255))
- May 15, 2026: died unexpectedly ([North Shore News obituary](https://www.legacy.com/ca/obituaries/nsnews/name/todd-pope-obituary?id=61598013))
- June 5, 2026: his community celebration of life was set for the same Capilano University library building where the award was later presented
- June 2026: the Sea to Sky Nationals BMX event was [dedicated to him](https://www.usabmx.com/news-and-media/General/2026-06-07/Squamish-BMX-hosts-Sea-to-Sky-Nationals-in-memory-of-Todd-Pope?id=2094)

## About the awards

A [2013 report](https://www.squamishreporter.com/2013/04/13/chamber-annouces-nominees-for-business-excellence-awards/) says Citizen of the Year was renamed for the late Bill Manson, a Chamber senator. Past winners include Amy Fast (2019), TlatlaKwot (Christine Baker) (2020), Carl Halvorson (2022) ([Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/squamish-business-excellence-awards-return-with-a-bang-6193279)) and Douglas Hackett (2025). [The 2025 gala was December 5, and more than 3,000 community members voted](https://www.pentictonherald.ca/spare_news/article_263d919e-5d6a-5920-b277-4452e3bf2da0.html).

For 2026, [nominations ran](https://squamishcc.awardify.io/) August 28 to September 18, and public voting ran October 9 to 23. The Legacy Award is not among the 12 categories on the [Chamber's awards page](https://www.squamishchamber.com/events-programming/business-excellence-awards/).

## What we don't know yet

- The Legacy Award's criteria, and who chose the recipient
- Whether it will be given again
- Who won Citizen of the Year in 2026

## A note on his wife's name

The Chamber's notice names his wife as Catherine. His [published obituary](https://www.squamishfuneralchapel.com/obituaries/Todd-Frederick-Pope?obId=48443876) names her as Caroline. We are seeking confirmation.

Source: [Squamish Chamber of Commerce](https://www.squamishchamber.com/).

stories.head: Squamish's new council just held its first real meeting. Here's everything that happened
stories.dek: The new council's first full meeting: a property tax freeze plan, a 4 to 2 split on co-living homes, steep slope rules and a flood plan grant. Every decision, who said what, and how to weigh in before December 1.
gist: Mayor Sean Easton wants the District to collect no more property tax in 2027 than it did in 2026; on December 1 council votes on whether to send staff back to rework the budget, and you can write to council@squamish.ca before then.

Staff say the current draft adds about $382 a year to the District part of an average home's bill, so a freeze means finding $6.3 million through higher fees, cuts or reserves, and new projects would wait until spring.

Council voted 4 to 2 to give business licences for co-living homes, where people rent rooms and share a kitchen, three of the four votes a bylaw needs; council's vote to adopt it comes at a later meeting. The mayor declared a conflict of interest, left the room and did not vote.
New steep slope rules and a flood plan grant passed with no one opposed.
stories.take: Nothing on the tax freeze is decided until December 1, and even then the budget itself comes later, by bylaw.

photo.alt: The mayor and six councillors in their camera tiles at the November 17 council meeting
photo.caption: The new council at its first full meeting, November 17. Top: Mayor Sean Easton, Laura Prosko, Janice DesJardins, Luc Perreault. Bottom: Shaun Veltkamp, Eric Andersen, Sarah Ellis.

fold.The tax freeze: No vote yet. Staff say a freeze means finding $6.3 million. Three members campaigned on a freeze; others urged caution or a slower path.
fold.Co-living homes: Three readings passed 4 to 2; adoption still to come. DesJardins and Perreault voted no and the mayor stepped out. Check whether your street's zone allows it.
fold.Steep slope rules: Adopted with no one opposed: a permit and an engineer's check for building on land at 30% slope or steeper. The old "no building over 40%" rule is gone.
fold.Flood plan grant: Approved with no one opposed: the District asks the Province for up to $200,000 toward updating its 2017 flood plan.
fold.Election report: Turnout was 45.33%, up from 39.73% in 2022. A second election day voting place is likely by 2030.
fold.How would you have voted?: Four quick yes or no questions, then see which council member voted most like you.
fold.What happens next: December 1: the tax freeze debate. Still to come: council's vote to adopt the co-living bylaw and an answer on the flood grant in March.
fold.Who spoke, and for how long: Staff spoke the most, about an hour. Among council, the mayor and Councillor Andersen, who each chaired part of the meeting, spoke longest. The tax freeze and co-living took about 40 and 27 minutes.

Province of BC, Community Charter section 165 and 197 (financial plan and tax rate deadlines)
Province of BC, Local Government Act section 470 (voting after a public hearing)
Province of BC, rent increase limits (2.2% for 2027)
stories.body:
## Every decision

[[glance]]

Each topic below shows how all seven voted. A red edge means the vote was split. Tap Read more for the details.

## The tax freeze

**In short:** The mayor wants no increase in District property tax for 2027. Staff say the draft adds about $382 to an average home, so a freeze means finding $6.3 million in fees, cuts or reserves. Council votes December 1 on whether to send staff back to rework the budget, and three of the seven campaigned on a freeze.

[[meeting card 2]]

[[meeting card 3]]

Mayor Easton's motion asks staff to rework the draft 2027 budget so the District collects **no more property tax than in 2026**. It also says services residents use must stay the same or get better, with no layoffs, no cut in union staff hours and no extra contracting out. Savings would come from a review of how the District is run, led by the chief administrative officer, with input from staff, unions and residents.

**Why he wants it.** "It's our turn to tighten our belts, like so many residents have had to in Squamish," he said, calling for "a leaner, meaner and more accountable government." He cited the District's own resident survey: only **37%** of residents felt they get good value for their municipal taxes, and **58%** said quality of life had dropped over five years. District tax has also climbed fast: compounded, the yearly increases from 2022 to 2026 put the total about **61%** above 2021 (our arithmetic), though part of that came from new buildings joining the tax roll.

[[bars levy]]

**What happens December 1.** Under council's procedure bylaw, a notice of motion comes up at the next regular meeting. Council can pass it, change it, send it elsewhere or defeat it. Passing it would send staff back to rework the draft; the budget itself is set later by bylaw. Three of the seven members campaigned on a 2027 freeze (Easton, DesJardins and Prosko), and a motion needs four votes when everyone is there; a 3 to 3 tie fails.

**Where each member stands.** Nobody voted on the freeze itself. Here is what each member said.

[[table stances]]

[[calc]]

Want your whole bill, including school, regional and hospital taxes? Try our [Squamish property tax calculator](/property-tax-calculator/).

**Renting?** You don't get a tax notice, but your landlord pays it. BC limits rent increases for current tenants to 2.2% in 2027, so a tax rise generally can't be passed on above that. The limit doesn't apply when a new tenancy starts. Some of the ways to close the gap, like higher recreation fees or smaller community grants, would reach renters directly.

**What staff say it would take.** The District's chief financial officer laid out the numbers. The draft collects about **$61 million** in property tax for daily services and repair savings, **$6.3 million more** than 2026. That's about **$382 a year**, or $32 a month, on an average home assessed at $1.2 million. Provincial law requires a balanced budget, so the District can't run a deficit: every dollar of a freeze has to come from somewhere.

[[table gap]]

About **$3.6 million** of that is already committed, mostly by contracts. So a freeze can't come from trimming this year's increase alone; staff would have to look at the whole operating budget.

[[table levers]]

The mayor's motion rules out layoffs and cuts to services residents use, so the main levers it leaves are fees, grants, special projects, reserves and the efficiency review.

**Timing.** If the motion passes, staff set the current draft aside while they rework it. Projects and purchases that haven't started would wait until a new plan is adopted, likely the end of March, which staff said shortens 2027 work plans by about a quarter. By law the financial plan comes first and the tax rate bylaw must be adopted before May 15.

**The review.** The general manager of corporate services said reviews like the one in the motion usually take about **a year**, cost about **$100,000** and are not usually done just to cut a budget. The last one started in 2019 and was finished in 2020. The chief administrative officer has announced their retirement, and staff noted a new one often reviews staffing structures anyway. The mayor answered that he isn't asking for a long review: he wants the people "closest to the issues" to find the savings.

[[bars towns]]

Councillor Ellis then moved that staff write a memo for December 1 on the timeline, costs, work put on hold and **scaled or phased options**. It passed with no one voting against it. DesJardins said she felt the extra motion wasn't needed, and Perreault worried about loading too much on staff at once.

[[poll freeze]]

## Co-living homes

**In short:** Licences for homes that rent rooms around a shared kitchen moved ahead 4 to 2, which lets fire and building staff inspect them. DesJardins and Perreault wanted more public input on parking and safety first; the others said inspections shouldn't wait. Council still has to vote to adopt the bylaw at a later meeting.

[[meeting card 0]]

[[meeting card 1]]

**The mayor stepped out.** Before the item, Mayor Easton declared a **conflict of interest**. He said he is a director of a non profit housing society that has a contract to buy a property with a co-living building on it. He left the room and Councillor Andersen, acting mayor for November, chaired. Under BC law, a member with a conflict must declare it, leave the room, stay out of the discussion and the vote, and not try to influence other members before or after.

Co-living means a long term home where people rent a private room and share the kitchen and living space. The previous council adopted the zoning rules in October. A bylaw passes in four steps: three readings, then a final vote called adoption. Council did all three readings in one vote, **4 to 2**. It lets the District issue business licences for co-living and send **fire and building staff to inspect**. Staff called it the last remaining piece: the zoning rules require an active licence, and until this bylaw passes there's no licence to get.

[[table coliving]]

[[zonecheck]]

**If you rent a room.** Once the bylaw gets its final vote, owners running co-living homes in these zones need a yearly licence, and fire and building staff can inspect. Homes are capped at 6 rented rooms and stays of 90 days or more. Staff said new co-living buildings would need the licence once they're finished. They didn't say on November 17 how existing shared houses will be brought in.

**The case for slowing down.** Councillor DesJardins moved to send "affordable workforce rental housing and the related parking requirements and neighbourhood planning" to council's strategic planning sessions, where council sets its priorities for the term. She said the rules allow co-living on **2,858 properties**, that the spring survey drew **62 responses** in a town of more than 20,000, and that **83%** of them worried about parking. She noted the fire department had warned about larger homes, and said Squamish has one co-living home in Dentville and another hoping to become one. "So let's get it right and let's do it with our residents, not around them," she said.

Councillor Perreault backed her. "I wanted to tell everyone from firsthand experience, there are challenges with co-living situations," he said, describing a co-living home near him whose tenants park some distance away.

**The case for going ahead.** Andersen said: "I think that there are risks in delaying the implementation bylaw. It allows for the relevant district staff to conduct inspections." Ellis said the motion's wording was broad enough to touch other kinds of housing. On the bylaw itself she said: "I don't believe the suite of regulations is perfect, but I do think it's worth advancing to understand and tweak as we go." She added that with the servicing rules and higher growth charges, co-living may now be **harder to build** than before, and the rules can be changed if they cause problems. Councillor Veltkamp said he agreed with her. Councillor Prosko asked staff one question and did not speak in the debate.

[[bars charges]]

DesJardins' motion **failed 2 to 4** (DesJardins and Perreault for; Andersen, Ellis, Prosko and Veltkamp against). The licence bylaw then **passed 4 to 2**, with DesJardins and Perreault against. Andersen then asked whether DesJardins' motion could come back as a separate item. The corporate officer said the procedure bylaw is silent on that and recommended a formal reconsideration vote instead, and it was left there.

**Next:** the licence bylaw needs its final vote, adoption, at a future meeting. BC law requires at least a day between third reading and adoption.

## Steep slope rules

**In short:** Building on land at 30% slope or steeper now needs a permit and an engineer's landslide check, approved by staff rather than council. The old ban on any building over 40% is gone. Existing homes on small lots are exempt.

[[meeting card 5]]

[[meeting card 6]]

Council gave final approval to a new **steep slope permit area** in the Official Community Plan, the town's long range land use plan. On land with an average slope of **30% or more**, you now need a permit, with a landslide hazard assessment by a qualified engineer, before you subdivide, build, dig or fill more than 1.2 metres, or cut trees 20 centimetres or wider. Lots of 0.2 hectares or smaller (about half an acre) that already have a house are exempt, and so is minor work. Private strata roads must now meet the District's public road grades, because steep roads slow down fire trucks.

[[slope]]

The bylaw also removes older limits from the plan: a slope report at 25%, no new single family houses on slopes of 25% or more, and **no development at all over 40%**. Staff said those caps didn't fit Squamish's short, rocky bluffs, and that the engineers they consulted saw "not a strong hazard mitigation rationale" for limits based on steepness alone. Not everyone agreed. An open house comment asked for a slope limit "above which development is not supported"; a third of the 45 spring survey replies called the visual design guidelines too onerous; and developers called the 30% line "too blunt". At the October public hearing, the one resident who spoke worried about how much rock and soil could be removed.

A planner said this finishes the last of six steps the 2018 plan requires before two future neighbourhood areas could be considered: District Lots 509 and 510 in the north, and land near Valleycliffe and the Mamquam area in the south. It does not approve any development there; each would still need its own applications. Hillside risk is real here: the new Cheekye debris flow barrier north of town cost more than $115 million, and a 2024 landslide in Lions Bay killed two people.

[[table slopes]]

Council also passed a second bylaw letting **District staff, not council, approve these permits**, the same way flood, wildfire and environmental permits are handled. Both passed with no one opposed. Only Andersen was on council at the October 6 public hearing. BC law lets members who missed a hearing vote on adoption once they get a report of what was said, and staff reminded the new council it can't take in new information on a bylaw after its hearing.

## Flood plan grant

**In short:** The District is asking the Province for up to $200,000 toward a $400,000 update of its 2017 flood plan. Staff said a Squamish River dike breach could displace over half the town.

[[meeting card 4]]

Squamish faces flooding from five river systems and the ocean, and its Integrated Flood Hazard Management Plan, the town's main guide for dikes and flood rules, dates from **2017**. It's due for its 10 year update, already budgeted at **$400,000 from District reserves** over 2027 and 2028. Council voted, with no one opposed, to apply to the Province's Community Emergency Preparedness Fund for up to **$200,000**, with a $100,000 ask in a second category as a backup; the District can win only one.

The stakes are high: engineering staff said a Squamish River dike breach "could displace over half of the community's residents and cause hundreds of millions of dollars in direct building damage." The District has won about $14 million in flood grants since the 2017 plan. Engineering staff said the new plan would move from mapping hazards to weighing risk, including sea level rise and new costs for dike upgrades. The application is due **Friday, November 20**, and staff expect an answer in March 2027; the program warns it will be heavily oversubscribed. It comes days after flooding washed out Squamish Valley Road and cut off the upper valley.

## Election report

**In short:** 45.33% of eligible voters cast a ballot in October, up from 39.73% in 2022 and well above the BC average.

[[meeting card 7]]

The corporate officer, who was also the chief election officer, reported on October's vote. Turnout was **45.33%**: 8,881 of 19,591 eligible voters, up from 39.73% in 2022 and well above the 29.2% BC average staff cited. Ballots cast rose about 32% from 2022 while eligible voters rose about 16% (our arithmetic). Advance voting rose to 2,932 people. Mayor Easton won by 175 votes. The election had a $120,000 budget, and staff expect Squamish will need a **second election day voting place by 2030**.

[[chart turnout]]

## Who spoke, and for how long

[[meeting talk]]

Councillor Andersen chaired the co-living item while the mayor was out, so part of his time was chairing too.

[[meeting time]]

## How would you have voted?

Four quick questions, one for each vote council took on November 17. Answer them and see which council member voted most like you.

[[match]]

## What happens next

- **December 1, 6 p.m.:** council debates the tax freeze motion, with the staff memo on costs and options. Write to council before then at council@squamish.ca, or send budget ideas to budgetfeedback@squamish.ca.
- **Co-living licences:** council's vote to adopt the bylaw, at a future meeting.
- **Flood grant:** application due November 20; an answer expected in March 2027.
- **Budget:** the District plans public input on the 2027 financial plan, which staff aim to finish by the end of March. By law, the financial plan comes before the tax rate bylaw, which must pass before May 15.

Watch any meeting live on the District's YouTube channel, or join by WebEx or phone (1-604-449-3026). Our [meeting page](/meetings/2026-11-17-regular/) has the full summary and transcript.

stories.head: St. Paul's residential school search starts next phase Nov. 23
stories.dek: The next phase of the search at the former St. Paul's Indian Residential School in North Vancouver begins Monday, November 23. The Squamish Nation's Yúusnew̓as team will clear brush on the school's old extended grounds, now a neighbourhood with homes on reserve land. The work will not disturb the soil, and data from the first phase is still being analyzed.
gist: The Squamish Nation's Yúusnew̓as project starts clearing brush on Monday, November 23, on land that was once part of St. Paul's residential school in North Vancouver.
The land is now a neighbourhood with private homes, and the work will not dig into the soil or make noise.
Data from the first phase is still being studied, and the Nation's project page labels the phases differently than the new notice does.
Questions can go to Yuusnewas@squamish.net, and the Nation's Wellness Department can be reached at 604-982-7816.

glance.v: Next to St. Thomas Aquinas, North Vancouver

stories.take: Brush clearing behind temporary fencing runs about one to two weeks from Monday, November 23, and people with questions can email Yuusnewas@squamish.net.
stories.body:
[[glance]]

Brush clearing starts Monday, November 23 on land next to St. Thomas Aquinas Regional Secondary School in North Vancouver. It is expected to run one to two weeks behind temporary fencing. The work will not disturb the soil, and the Nation says it should not make noise or cause a disturbance.

The work is part of Yúusnew̓as, a project led by the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh (Squamish Nation) community that researches and documents the residential school experiences of the Nation's people. It is the next phase of groundwork at the former St. Paul's Indian Residential School.

## What happens now

The land was once the extended grounds of St. Paul's. It is now a residential neighbourhood on Squamish Nation reserve land, home to several private residences. The original school site is now a staff parking lot at St. Thomas Aquinas. The old school stood in the City of North Vancouver; this land is Squamish Nation reserve land in North Vancouver, not in the District of Squamish ([Daily Hive](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/investigation-st-pauls-residential-school-north-vancouver)).

- Start: Monday, November 23
- Length: one to two weeks
- Work: light brush clearing on the surface that will not disturb the soil
- Temporary fencing while the work is underway
- No noise or disturbance expected

Before the work, the Yúusnew̓as Family will hold a ceremony to announce it to the Ancestors. No date was given for the ceremony. The notice does not name the streets or lots affected. Questions can go to Yuusnewas@squamish.net.

If this news is hard to read, the Nation's Háhalhi7iwan (Wellness) Department is at 604-982-7816. Full contacts are below.

## Phase one: data still being analyzed

The first phase of groundwork took place on the site of the former school in 2023 and 2024. The team used:

- LiDAR: laser scans that map the shape of the ground
- Ground penetrating radar: radio waves that look for changes below the surface
- Electrical resistivity: measuring how easily electricity passes through the ground
- Percussion coring: driving a narrow tube into the ground to pull out soil
- Soil sampling

In April 2024 the Nation said it had collected more than 50 million data points. It said the data showed "several areas of interest" that need more study, and that the scan results "are inconclusive and do not indicate burials" ([Squamish Nation newsletter, April 2024](https://www.squamish.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/SV-Newsletter_April-25-2024.pdf)).

The new notice says the work and the site are complicated, so it takes time to read the data accurately. The project is moving ahead while the team waits for findings.

The notice calls the November work the second phase. The Nation's [Yúusnew̓as project page](https://www.squamish.net/community-initiatives/yuusnewas/) says the Nation is waiting for results from "the second phase of land-based work" done "last summer." The notice does not explain the difference.

## Why the search started

- 1899 to September 1, 1959: St. Paul's operates ([National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation](https://archives.nctr.ca/St-Pauls-Residential-School-Squamish)). It was Metro Vancouver's only residential school ([Global News](https://globalnews.ca/news/8100397/st-pauls-residential-school-north-vancouver/))
- 1904 to 1913: public records show 12 unidentified students died while attending ([Musqueam](https://www.musqueam.bc.ca/st-pauls-investigation-announcement/))
- Some students were later forcibly sent to Kamloops Indian Residential School ([Daily Hive](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/investigation-st-pauls-residential-school-north-vancouver))
- August 10, 2021: the Squamish, Musqueam and Tsleil-Waututh Nations announce the investigation, with support from the Catholic Archdiocese of Vancouver ([Georgia Straight](https://www.straight.com/news/squamish-musqueam-and-tsleil-waututh-nations-announce-probe-into-former-indian-residential))
- 2023 to 2024: phase one groundwork
- November 23, 2026: brush clearing begins

The Squamish Nation leads the project in close partnership with Tsleil-Waututh and Musqueam. It has four parts: ground investigation, archival research, health and wellness, and recording syets (truths) from Survivors ([Squamish Nation](https://www.squamish.net/community-initiatives/yuusnewas/)).

## Money

Ottawa's Residential Schools Missing Children Community Support Fund has three streams: research, commemoration and field investigation ([Government of Canada](https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1647884354823/1647884389372)). As of February 2026 it had signed 164 agreements worth $280 million in total ([Government of Canada](https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1772740539781/1772740559094)). In a [federal budget brief](https://www.ourcommons.ca/Content/Committee/441/FINA/Brief/BR13229900/br-external/SquamishNationGovernment-e.pdf), the Squamish Nation asked Canada to remove a newly announced cap on this funding. We could not find how much Yúusnew̓as itself has received.

## Questions the notice leaves open

- When phase one findings will be released
- Why this neighbourhood was chosen
- What follows the brush clearing
- What this phase costs

## Questions and wellness supports

- Project questions: Yuusnewas@squamish.net
- Háhalhi7iwan (Wellness) Department: Wellness@squamish.net, 604-982-7816
- Mackenzie Gomez, Yúusnew̓as Health Lead: Mackenzie_Gomez@squamish.net, 604-360-3911 or 604-982-7816
- Hannah Rushton, Yúusnew̓as Wellness Lead: Hannah_Rushton@squamish.net, 778-233-4869 or 604-985-4111

Read the [Squamish Nation notice](https://www.squamish.net/yuusnew%cc%93as-to-begin-second-phase-of-groundwork-in-november/).

stories.head: Going home after this month's floods? Seven steps first, and who to call
stories.dek: If floodwater reached your home, farm or well, the regional district's new guide says what to do before you clean up or turn the power back on. The Squamish-Lillooet Regional District released the webpage and guide on November 17. It covers safety, cleanup, wells and septic, insurance, permits, farms and mental health.
gist: The regional district has put out a new guide for people going back to homes hit by this month's floods.
Take photos and video of damage before you clear anything, and call your insurer as soon as you can.
Dangers can remain after the water goes down, so a professional must check power or gas systems that floodwater reached before you use them.
We could not find any announcement that the province will help pay for damage from this flood.
stories.take: Photograph damage before you remove debris, call your insurer as soon as possible, and keep power and gas off until a qualified professional inspects them.
stories.body:
[[glance]]
Rain and river figures in the tiles come from [the Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/stay-back-from-riverbanks-district-of-squamish-warns-of-erosion-after-flooding-13010625).

## Seven things to do first
This month's floods hit homes, farms and neighbourhoods across the region, including the Squamish Valley, Paradise Valley, the Sunwolf Lodge and Cheekye Ranch area, the Pemberton Valley and Lílwat Nation lands. On November 17 the Squamish-Lillooet Regional District released a [Returning Home After a Flood webpage and guide](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/protective-emergency-services/recovery/flood-return-home). Some evacuation alerts have been lifted, but the regional district warns hazards may remain after the water goes down. Its key reminders:

- Only go home when it is safe, and follow any evacuation and access rules.
- Do not enter a building with standing floodwater or signs of damage to its structure.
- Take photos and video of the damage before you remove any debris.
- Contact your insurer as soon as possible.
- Do not turn electrical or gas systems back on if floodwater reached them, until a qualified professional inspects them.
- If floodwater reached your private well, use another safe water source until the well is checked and restored. The [guide](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/protective-emergency-services/recovery/flood-return-home) also covers septic safety.
- Dry wet areas as soon as it is safe, to prevent mould.

The guide also covers debris disposal, repairs and building permits, farm support, help for renters, mental health and a recovery checklist. We could not confirm whether it applies inside District of Squamish limits. Town residents can call the District's Emergency Operations Centre at 778-655-3020, [the Squamish Chief reported](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/flood-alert-residents-told-to-shelter-in-place-in-paradise-valley-12935070).

## Roads and riverbanks
As of November 13, EmergencyInfoBC said [Squamish Valley Road was closed](https://www.emergencyinfobc.gov.bc.ca/event/shelter-in-place-squamish-12nov26/) at the Cheakamus River Bridge (Fergies) and at a washout just before Tantalus Acres: "The road is impassable. Do not travel down the road and do not attempt to cross." We found no later update. Check for the latest at [www.slrd.bc.ca/eoc](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/eoc) and [EmergencyInfoBC](https://www.emergencyinfobc.gov.bc.ca/event/shelter-in-place-squamish-12nov26/).

The District of Squamish is [urging people to stay away from riverbanks](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/stay-back-from-riverbanks-district-of-squamish-warns-of-erosion-after-flooding-13010625), because falling water leaves erosion and unstable ground. The District said road flooding should stop once the Brackendale gauge drops below 450 cubic metres per second. Check the current reading on our [today page](/today/).

## Timeline, November 12 to 17
- November 12: BC Hydro issued a flood alert below the Cheakamus Dam (Daisy Lake), and Paradise Valley residents were told to shelter in place ([Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/flood-alert-residents-told-to-shelter-in-place-in-paradise-valley-12935070)).
- November 12: Three people died after a boat crashed on the Squamish River ([CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/3-dead-squamish-boating-incident-9.7420872)).
- November 13: The Squamish Nation said about 40 members were evacuated from homes in the Squamish Valley ([Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/stay-back-from-riverbanks-district-of-squamish-warns-of-erosion-after-flooding-13010625)).
- By November 13: The advisory for Paradise Valley and the Sunwolf Lodge and Cheekye Ranch area ended. Paradise Valley Road reopened at the Bailey Bridge with one lane of alternating traffic ([EmergencyInfoBC](https://www.emergencyinfobc.gov.bc.ca/event/shelter-in-place-squamish-12nov26/)).
- November 15, 3:30 p.m.: The regional district [cancelled the Pemberton Valley evacuation alert](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/inside-slrd/news-notices/evacuation-alert-rescind-electoral-area-c-pemberton-valley).
- November 16: Lílwat Nation evacuation orders remained for about 20 properties with submerged septic systems or other unsafe conditions ([CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/bc-storm-nov-15-9.7423108)).
- November 17: The regional district released its return home guide.

## Who pays for damage?
We could not find any announcement of Disaster Financial Assistance for this flood. Under the [province's past rules](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/safety/emergency-management/preparedbc/evacuation-recovery/disaster-financial-assistance):

- 80% of eligible damage, less $1,000, up to $400,000 under past rules; not announced for this flood.
- It covers only losses that could not be insured.
- The home must have been your main residence. Seasonal or recreational properties do not qualify, and landlords apply as small businesses.

For reference, after the December 10 to 19, 2025 floods, people had until April 13, 2026 to apply, and the help line was 1-888-257-4777 ([B.C. Gov News](https://news.gov.bc.ca/releases/2026EMCR0001-000027)).

## What we don't know yet
- Whether the province will open Disaster Financial Assistance for this flood, and any deadline
- How many homes, wells or farms were damaged
- When Squamish Valley Road will reopen
- Whether Squamish Nation members have different steps for returning home

## Who to call
- Immediate danger: 911
- Regional district Duty Officer, 24 hours a day, for flood concerns: 604-384-7357
- District of Squamish Emergency Operations Centre: 778-655-3020
- Regional district Agricultural Coordinator (farms): 604-384-7329
- Emergency Support Services through the Canadian Red Cross: 1-888-800-6493
- Emergency updates: [www.slrd.bc.ca/eoc](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/eoc)
- Flood advisories: BC River Forecast Centre

The regional district encourages residents to sign up for SLRD Alert to get emergency notices by phone, text or email. Follow flood news on our [flood protection page](/issues/flood-protection/).

stories.head: Animals or farm hit by flooding or evacuation? Call this number for help
stories.dek: Flooding and evacuation measures can leave farm animals and livestock in trouble. Farmers, ranchers and livestock owners can call the Squamish-Lillooet Regional District's Agricultural Coordinator directly for help.
stories.take: If flooding or an evacuation affects your animals or farm, call the Agricultural Coordinator at 604-384-7329.
stories.body:
## Who to call

The Squamish-Lillooet Regional District (SLRD) announced this on November 15. Farmers, ranchers and livestock owners affected by flooding or evacuation measures can contact the SLRD's Agricultural Coordinator directly. The coordinator helps with moving and caring for livestock and other animals, and other farm emergency needs.

- Phone: SLRD Agricultural Coordinator, 604-384-7329
- Who can call: farmers, ranchers and livestock owners affected by flooding or evacuation measures
- What for: coordinating livestock, animals or other agriculture-related emergency needs

## Check conditions now

If you are deciding whether to move animals, check [current river levels, weather and Highway 99 on our today page](/today/). For background on flooding in our area, see [our flood protection issue page](/issues/flood-protection/).

## Planning help online

The SLRD has an Agricultural Emergency Preparedness page on its website. It includes:

- Premises ID sign up
- Evacuation checklists
- Livestock relocation information

## Source

Read the original [SLRD news release](https://e1.envoke.com/ext/click/go/72b42360f6f117b691464136292515ef/208354e17f0578d1a016afa1289bcee0/6cd9fbfbbbbeeabe00dc6e15657d2f75).

stories.head: Up to 70 mm more rain possible by Sunday night. Why soaked ground matters
stories.dek: Ground already soaked by this week's storms can't absorb as much water, which could make this next round of heavy rain worse. Environment Canada has a rainfall warning for Howe Sound and the Sea-to-Sky. 40 to 70 mm is possible from late Saturday afternoon through Sunday night.
stories.take: From late Saturday afternoon through Sunday night, drive with care and watch for pooled water, visibility that can drop suddenly, and washouts near rivers, creeks and culverts.
stories.body:
Environment Canada issued a rainfall warning Saturday, November 14 for Howe Sound and the Sea-to-Sky. 40 to 70 mm of rain is possible, starting late Saturday afternoon and continuing through Sunday night.

Check river levels, Highway 99 and current weather on our [today page](/today/).

## What to watch for

The warning lists these risks during the heavy rain:

- Water pooling on roads and in low spots
- Visibility that can drop suddenly at times
- Washouts near rivers, creeks and culverts

## Why this round matters

This is a new storm system full of moisture heading for the B.C. coast, bringing another round of significant rain to the west coast. The heavy rain is expected to begin late Saturday afternoon and keep going through Sunday.

The ground is already saturated from a series of storms earlier in the week. Soaked ground can't absorb as much water, which the forecasters say could make the impacts of this rain worse. You can read more about local flood risk on our [flood protection issue page](/issues/flood-protection/).

## Stay up to date

Forecasters ask people to keep checking alerts and forecasts as the system moves in.

To report severe weather, email BCstorm@ec.gc.ca or post on social media using #BCStorm.

Read the full warning on the [Environment Canada website](https://weather.gc.ca/warnings/index_e.html?prov=bc).

## What is happening

Repairs on the Paradise Valley Bailey Bridge are still under way, the District of Squamish said in its November 13 [E-News](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/enews-archives/). Overnight closures are expected while crews do the work.

The District has not given dates or times for the closures. If you rely on the bridge at night, plan for the chance that it may be closed. The District posts updates in its E-News.

## The bridge abutments

The abutments are the supports at each end of the bridge. Replacing them is a separate step from the repairs now under way, and the District has not given a schedule for it. The District says more on replacing the abutments will be shared when available, after the current weather event.

While the District waits for the weather event to pass, you can check river levels on our [today page](/today/).

## Dike and pump station work

The District also lists this work continuing through November:

- Phased construction on the Squamish River Dike at the Harris and Dryden Pump Stations
- Work at the Central Lift Station

The District did not describe what the Central Lift Station work involves. For more on how Squamish manages its dikes, see our [flood protection](/issues/flood-protection/) issue page.

stories.head: Squamish Nation asks people to stay away as Notcho the whale moves inland
stories.dek: The Squamish Nation says the area where Notcho has been resting is now an active work site and is no longer safe to visit. The Nation has begun moving Notcho, a humpback whale struck and killed by a BC Ferry, from his resting spot on the beach to a new spot further inland using heavy machinery. A ceremony for his final burial on Squamish Nation territory will follow once the work is done.
stories.take: The Squamish Nation will hold a ceremony for Notcho's final burial on its territory once the move is finished, and says it will share the ceremony details as soon as they are available.
stories.body:
## What is happening

The area where Notcho has been resting is now an active work site and is no longer safe to visit, so the Squamish Nation asks people to stay away. In an update posted Nov. 13, Chairperson Sxwíxwtn Wilson Williams said the Nation has begun the challenging work of moving Notcho, a humpback whale, from his resting spot on the beach to a new spot further inland.

Moving Notcho is a difficult job that needs heavy machinery. The request is worded to "Community," asking them to respect the work and not go to the area. The Nation says that respect and patience will ensure Notcho can provide ongoing gifts and teachings for its community for years to come.

The update does not name the beach, give an end date for the work, or set a date for the ceremony.

## Why the Nation is caring for Notcho

Notcho was struck and killed by a BC Ferry in the Nation's territorial waters. In Sḵwx̱wú7mesh sníchim (the Squamish language), whales are called Ḵwenís, and the Nation calls them sacred relatives.

The update says it was the Nation's responsibility to support Notcho on his new journey. It says Squamish People have been stewards of these waters since time immemorial, and that caring for Notcho is that stewardship in action. It also says Notcho has given the community a chance to reconnect with ancient cultural practices and keep learning.

## Who is helping

Volunteers are coming together to help with the next phase of the work:

- The University of British Columbia
- The Beatty Biodiversity Museum
- The Vancouver Aquarium
- Several members of the Squamish Nation community

## What comes next

The work must be finished before the Nation can hold a ceremony to mark Notcho's final burial on its territory. The Nation says it will share ceremony details as soon as they are available.

Read the full update from the [Squamish Nation](https://www.squamish.net/caring-for-notcho-a-journey-of-stewardship-and-respect/). For more local environment stories, see our [climate and environment](/issues/climate-and-environment/) page.
stories.social:

Notcho was struck and killed by a BC Ferry. Volunteers from the University of British Columbia, the Beatty Biodiversity Museum, the Vancouver Aquarium and Nation members are helping with the next phase of the work, which must be finished before a final burial ceremony.

stories.head: Two dead, one missing in Squamish Valley boat incident. Stay off the water
stories.dek: Two people have died and one person is still missing after a boat incident in the Squamish Valley on the afternoon of November 12. High water and bad weather made the first day's search extremely difficult and unsafe for responders, and search, rescue and recovery work is continuing today (Friday). Squamish RCMP are asking everyone to stay off the water.
stories.take: Squamish RCMP are asking everyone to stay off the water because of dangerous flow rates and debris throughout the river systems.
stories.body:
## What happened

Squamish RCMP responded to a boat incident in the Squamish Valley at about 1:52 p.m. on Thursday, November 12, 2026. Several people were involved.

Police say two people have been confirmed dead and one person is still missing. Everyone else involved has been accounted for.

Search, rescue and recovery operations are continuing on Friday, November 13.

Police have not said which river or where in the valley it happened, or how many people were on board. They say no more information will be released at this time.

## What police are asking

"We are asking the public to stay off the water at this time due to dangerous flow rates and debris throughout the river systems," said Cpl. Ashley MacKay of the Squamish RCMP.

For current river levels, see our [today page](/today/).

## Why the search is hard

Water levels were high and the weather was poor on November 12. Police say this made search, rescue and recovery work extremely difficult and unsafe for emergency crews, so the work carried on the next day.

"The weather and river conditions have played a significant role in the response efforts," MacKay said. She called it "a very dynamic and evolving incident" and said "the safety of responders and the public remains paramount."

MacKay said weather, water levels and river conditions can change quickly. Those conditions are being checked all the time as the search goes on.

## Who is helping

RCMP call this a time-sensitive and complex response. Squamish RCMP have brought in:

- Squamish Search and Rescue
- RCMP Air Services
- Lower Mainland District Integrated Emergency Response Team
- RCMP Underwater Recovery Team
- West Coast Marine Services

Read the [RCMP news release](https://rcmp.ca/en/bc/squamish/news/2026/11/4358753) (file 2026-10050). Media contact: Cpl. Ashley MacKay, 604-892-6100.
